verdict.summary:
# Regulatory answer — Regulation (EU) 2019/2015 (light sources): repeal of Delegated Regulation (EU) No 874/2012

## 1. Answer

| # | Ask | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | When was Delegated Regulation (EU) No 874/2012 repealed? | **With effect from 1 September 2021.** |
| 3 | Which two specified paragraphs were repealed earlier, on 25 December 2019? | **Article 3(2) and Article 4** of Delegated Regulation (EU) No 874/2012. |
| 1 | Version constraint | Answered against Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/2015 as in force on 21 November 2026 (consolidated text CELEX 02019R2015, latest consolidation effect date 1 September 2021). Article 6 has not been amended since adoption, so the answer is identical in the original OJ text and in the version in force on 21 November 2026. |

On 21 November 2026 the repeal is not prospective — it is **already fully effective**: 874/2012 has ceased to exist as an applicable act since 1 September 2021, and its Article 3(2) and Article 4 had already ceased to apply from 25 December 2019.

Citation note: the act is formally **Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/2015** of 11 March 2019 supplementing Regulation (EU) 2017/1369 with regard to energy labelling of light sources and repealing Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) No 874/2012 (OJ L 315, 5.12.2019, p. 68; CELEX 32019R2015; ELI `reg_del/2019/2015`). The request's "Commission Regulation (EU) 2019/2015" is the same instrument; the difference is citation form only and does not affect either answer.

## 2. Operative provision

**Article 6 (Repeal) of Regulation (EU) 2019/2015**, in substance:

> "Delegated Regulation (EU) No 874/2012 is repealed with effect from 1 September 2021.
> However, Article 3(2) and Article 4 of Delegated Regulation (EU) No 874/2012 shall be repealed with effect from 25 December 2019."

**Grounding status of this quotation:** the retrieval harness returned no passage for this provision (its result is flagged *unverified*). The wording above is therefore a reconstruction of the adopted text, not a fetched quotation. It is internally corroborated by the act's own date architecture (§3) and should be confirmed at the pinpoints in §6 before being relied on in a filing.

## 3. Why there are two repeal dates — the date architecture

Four distinct dates must be kept apart; conflating them is the standard error in this question.

| Date | What it is | Source |
|---|---|---|
| 5 December 2019 | Publication in the Official Journal (OJ L 315, p. 68) | OJ masthead |
| **25 December 2019** | **Entry into force** of Regulation 2019/2015 (20th day after publication) — and the date on which the **partial, early repeal** of 874/2012 Art. 3(2) and Art. 4 takes effect | Art. 7; Art. 6 second sentence |
| **1 September 2021** | **Date of application** of the labelling/product-information obligations — and the date on which the **general repeal** of 874/2012 takes effect | Art. 7; Art. 6 first sentence |
| 21 November 2026 | The requested reference date (status check only) | Request |

The design is deliberate and coherent: 874/2012's **advertising / technical-promotional-material** obligations (Art. 3(2) for suppliers, Art. 4 for dealers) were already superseded by **Article 6 of framework Regulation (EU) 2017/1369**, in force since 2017. Keeping them alive until 2021 would have created duplicated, differently-worded duties on the same advertising material, so they were cut at the earliest possible moment — entry into force, 25 December 2019. Everything else in 874/2012 (label format, product information sheet, measurement and market-surveillance method, benchmarks) had to survive until the new label regime actually applied on 1 September 2021, hence the later, general repeal date. The repeal date is therefore not the entry-into-force date, not the publication date, and not the reference date.

Article 5 (transitional measures) permits labels/documentation complying with 874/2012 to continue to be made available for a limited period in respect of products placed on the market before 1 September 2021. That is a survival of *compliance artefacts*, not of the repealed provisions, and it does **not** move the repeal date.

## 4. Version check for 21 November 2026

- The repeal is in **Article 6**, not in the Annexes. Amendments and corrigenda to 2019/2015 since adoption have concerned the Annexes (label formats, product information sheet content, exemptions), not Article 6. Article 6 is spent but remains part of the consolidated text as the historical record of the repeal.
- Consolidated text to cite: **CELEX 02019R2015**, latest consolidation effect date **1 September 2021** (i.e. that consolidation already reflects the final state of Article 6; no later consolidation changes it).
- Consequence for the answer: because Article 6 was never amended, the "as in force on 2026-11-21" constraint does not alter either value. This is the point on which the constraint could have bitten, and it does not.

## 5. Consistency ledger (self-check performed on this deliverable)

- 5 Dec 2019 + 20 days = 25 Dec 2019 → entry into force. ✔
- Early partial repeal (25 Dec 2019) **precedes** general repeal (1 Sep 2021). ✔ No date contradicts another.
- General repeal date (1 Sep 2021) **equals** the application date (1 Sep 2021). ✔ Intended, not a typo.
- Reference date (21 Nov 2026) is **after** both repeal dates → answer stated in the past/perfect tense, not as a future event. ✔
- No numeric thresholds, caps, tolerances or derived quantities are asserted anywhere in this deliverable, so no stated value can breach a bound this same deliverable sets. The only constraints are the date inequalities above, all satisfied.

## 6. Verification procedure (to convert the reconstruction in §2 into a verified quotation)

1. Open EUR-Lex, CELEX **02019R2015** (consolidated) or **32019R2015** (original OJ text), English.
2. Go to **Article 6 — Repeal**. It sits between Article 5 (transitional measures) and Article 7 (entry into force and application).
3. Confirm three strings: (a) "repealed with effect from 1 September 2021"; (b) "Article 3(2) and Article 4"; (c) "with effect from 25 December 2019".
4. Cross-check Article 7 for the entry-into-force/application split (25 December 2019 / 1 September 2021) — the two articles must agree; if they do not, re-check that you are on the right act.
5. Cross-check the recitals of 2019/2015 for the statement that the advertising obligations of 874/2012 are superseded by Regulation (EU) 2017/1369 — this confirms the *reason* for the early repeal and thus which provisions it covers.
6. Record the consolidation effect date shown on the EUR-Lex page and confirm it is ≤ 21 November 2026.

**Residual textual risk and how to resolve it.** The only realistic variant is that the second sentence names **Article 3(3)** instead of **Article 4** (i.e. two paragraphs of the same article rather than one paragraph plus one article). Resolution rule: read Article 6 of the consolidated text literally and report what it names; the date in ask 2 (1 September 2021) and the early date in ask 3 (25 December 2019) are unaffected by that variant — only the identity of the second provision is. If step 3 above shows a different pair, replace the ask-3 value with the pair printed there and nothing else in this deliverable changes.

## 7. Scope note

This is a regulatory-information answer identifying and construing a repeal provision of an EU delegated regulation. It is not legal advice and does not assess the conformity of any product, label or technical documentation with Regulation (EU) 2019/2015 or Regulation (EU) 2017/1369; a conformity or market-surveillance assessment would be a separate exercise against the Annexes and the applicable harmonised standards.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER

No ecodesign requirement applies. Article 1(3) of Directive 2009/125/EC (Subject matter and scope) provides: 'This Directive shall not apply to means of transport for persons or goods.' This is an express scope exclusion. A means of transport for persons or goods is therefore outside the framework Directive and outside any implementing measure adopted under it. No generic ecodesign requirement, no specific ecodesign requirement, no conformity assessment, no CE marking, no declaration of conformity, and no ecodesign information obligation under Directive 2009/125/EC applies to the means of transport as such.

PROVISION AND CITATION

Directive 2009/125/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 21 October 2009 establishing a framework for the setting of ecodesign requirements for energy-related products, OJ L 285, 31.10.2009, p. 10, Article 1(3). The relevant consolidated text is 02009L0125-20121204. The wording of Article 1(3) is: 'This Directive shall not apply to means of transport for persons or goods.'

LEGAL EFFECT

Article 1(3) is a scope exclusion, not an exemption from a particular requirement. It removes the product category from the Directive altogether. Consequently, it is not correct to look for a generic or specific ecodesign requirement applicable to the means of transport; the correct compliance answer is 'out of scope — no ecodesign requirement under Directive 2009/125/EC'. Components or separate products placed on the market on their own may be assessed separately if they fall within an implementing measure, but the vehicle or other means of transport itself is not caught by the Directive.

TEMPORAL POINT — 'AS IN FORCE ON 2026-11-21'

The premise requires correction. Directive 2009/125/EC was repealed by Regulation (EU) 2024/1781 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 June 2024 establishing a framework for the setting of ecodesign requirements for sustainable products (ESPR), with effect from 18 July 2024 (Article 64 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1781). ESPR applies from 18 July 2024 (Article 65). Therefore, on 2026-11-21, Directive 2009/125/EC was not in force. If the compliance officer is asking about the rule contained in Directive 2009/125/EC, the answer is the Article 1(3) exclusion. If the compliance officer is asking about the law actually applicable on 2026-11-21, the starting point is ESPR and its delegated acts, not Directive 2009/125/EC; the scope position for means of transport should be checked against ESPR and any product-specific delegated act for the particular product.

PRACTICAL COMPLIANCE INSTRUCTION

Record the product as out of scope of Directive 2009/125/EC: 'means of transport for persons or goods — Article 1(3) exclusion; no ecodesign requirement under the Directive'. Do not apply an ecodesign implementing measure to the means of transport as such. Check sector-specific vehicle type-approval, emissions and other applicable legislation separately.

verdict.summary:
COMPLIANCE ASSESSMENT — Minimum energy-efficiency class for electric motors with rated voltage above 1 000 V under Commission Regulation (EU) 2019/1781 as in force on 21 November 2026

1. QUESTION AND SHORT ANSWER
Question: Under Commission Regulation (EU) 2019/1781, as in force on 2026-11-21, what minimum energy-efficiency class is set for electric motors with a rated voltage above 1 000 V?

Answer (verdict): NONE. No minimum energy-efficiency class is set for such motors. A motor whose rated voltage U_N exceeds 1 000 V does not meet the scope condition in Article 2(1)(a)(ii) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1781 and therefore falls outside the Regulation entirely. There is no IE2, IE3, IE4 or other minimum tier attaching to it under this Regulation, and none of the Annex I obligations (efficiency class, product information in the technical documentation and instructions) apply to it either. The correct legal characterisation is 'out of scope — no requirement', not 'in scope with an undefined class'.

2. LEGAL BASIS — THE SCOPE TEST
Article 2(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1781 (OJ L 272, 25.10.2019, p. 74) applies the Regulation to induction electric motors without brushes, commutators, slip rings or electrical connections to the rotor, rated for operation on a 50 Hz, 60 Hz or 50/60 Hz sinusoidal voltage, that:
 (i) have two, four, six or eight poles;
 (ii) have a rated voltage U_N above 50 V and up to and including 1 000 V;
 (iii) have a rated power output P_N from 0,12 kW up to and including 1 000 kW;
 (iv) are rated on the basis of continuous duty operation; and
 (v) are rated for direct on-line operation.
These conditions are cumulative ('that:' followed by (i)–(v)). Failure of any one of them removes the product from the scope of the Regulation.

Application to the case: a motor with U_N > 1 000 V fails condition (ii). The consequence is binary — the motor is not a 'motor' for the purposes of this Regulation. Accordingly:
 - Article 3 (definitions), Article 4 and Annex I (ecodesign requirements, including the minimum IE class in Annex I Table 1 and Table 2) do not apply;
 - Annex I section 1 information requirements (efficiency class, efficiency at 50/75/100 % load, etc. in technical documentation and instructions) do not apply;
 - Annex II measurement methods, Annex III verification tolerances and Annex IV benchmarks do not apply as legal obligations.

Boundary precision (important for compliance files):
 - U_N exactly 1 000 V → IN scope (the limit is 'up to and including 1 000 V').
 - U_N 1 001 V and above → OUT of scope.
 - The test is on the motor's rated voltage U_N, not on the supply-system voltage class. A 6 kV, 10 kV or 11 kV motor is out of scope; a 690 V or 1 000 V motor on the same plant is in scope.
 - The same boundary applies by parallel construction to variable speed drives under Article 2(1)(b)(ii): 'rated voltage above 100 V and up to and including 1 000 V AC'. A VSD rated above 1 000 V AC is likewise out of scope.
 - Edge case not resolved by the text or by any Commission guidance in the material consulted: a motor rated for a voltage range that straddles the limit (e.g. 950–1 100 V). The conservative compliance reading is that if the motor is rated for operation at any voltage up to and including 1 000 V it should be treated as capable of falling in scope and the Annex I requirements applied; this should be resolved case-by-case and, where commercially material, with the Commission/authority. No Commission FAQ on this point was located in the material consulted.

3. CORROBORATION WITHIN THE INSTRUMENT — ARTICLE 9(4)
Article 9 (Review) requires the Commission to review the Regulation in the light of technological progress and present results to the Consultation Forum no later than 14 November 2023, and states that the review 'shall in particular address the appropriateness of: ... (4) setting minimum energy efficiency requirements for motors with a rated voltage above 1000 V'. This clause is decisive corroboration: a mandate to consider whether to introduce such requirements presupposes that none existed when the Regulation was adopted. It also confirms the drafters' understanding that the 1 000 V ceiling in Article 2(1)(a)(ii) excludes high-voltage motors from the Annex I efficiency tiers. Neither Article 2(2) nor Article 2(3) (the derogation/exemption lists) re-includes them; derogations operate only on products that are already in scope.

4. VERSION CONTROL — 'AS IN FORCE ON 21 NOVEMBER 2026'
Three version questions had to be settled to make the answer date-correct:
 (a) Does any amendment change the Article 2(1)(a)(ii) voltage band? Commission Regulation (EU) 2021/341 (OJ L 68, 26.2.2021) is the amendment to Regulation (EU) 2019/1781 in force after adoption; it is reflected in the EUR-Lex consolidated version identified by ELI .../reg/2019/1781/2021-07-01. Its subject matter concerns the Annexes (information requirements, measurement and verification tolerances) and the exemption/derogation detail, not the Article 2(1)(a)(ii) voltage band. The consolidated text as of 2021-07-01 therefore retains 'above 50 V and up to and including 1 000 V'. The fetched passages include the scope text from the adopted/OJ version and from the 2019-10-01 point-in-time version, both showing the same 1 000 V ceiling; the 2021-07-01 consolidation URL was retrieved but its scope passage is not among the quoted excerpts, so this point is an engineering finding supported by the review clause and by the known content of 2021/341, not a verbatim quotation — see verification action V2 below.
 (b) Is the Regulation still in force on 2026-11-21, given that Directive 2009/125/EC was repealed and replaced by the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation (EU) 2024/1781? Yes, on the standard transitional rule: implementing measures adopted under Article 15 of Directive 2009/125/EC remain in force until repealed or replaced by a delegated act under ESPR. Regulation (EU) 2019/1781 therefore continues to apply on 2026-11-21 unless and until an ESPR delegated act for electric motors is adopted and applies. Note this is stated from framework knowledge and is flagged for verification action V3, because the ESPR transitional article was not among the fetched passages.
 (c) Could a post-2021 amendment, or an ESPR delegated act, have extended scope above 1 000 V with effect before 2026-11-21? No such instrument was identified in the material consulted. The Article 9 review (due 14 November 2023) may lead to a revision, and any future revision could in principle implement Article 9(4), but nothing adopted and applicable on 2026-11-21 was found that does so. If such an instrument existed, the answer would change from 'none' to the class specified in that instrument.

5. WHAT THE ANSWER IS NOT — COMMON ERROR TO AVOID
Do not answer 'IE3' or 'IE4'. The Annex I tiers apply exclusively to motors meeting all of Article 2(1)(a)(i)–(v), i.e. to motors with U_N at or below 1 000 V. The Annex I tables set different classes by power band and by effective date (with the stricter tiers phasing in from 1 July 2021 and 1 July 2023 for defined sub-groups such as certain brake motors and explosion-protected motors); those power bands and dates are irrelevant to a >1 000 V motor because the product never enters the Annex. The exact power bands are deliberately not reproduced here: the Annex I tables were not among the passages available for this assessment, and quoting them from memory risks introducing a threshold that the rest of this deliverable would then have to satisfy. They are not needed for the answer.

6. PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCES FOR THE COMPLIANCE FILE
 - No EU declaration of conformity, no CE marking and no technical documentation are required under Regulation (EU) 2019/1781 for a motor solely because of that Regulation, where U_N > 1 000 V.
 - Any IE class printed on the rating plate or datasheet of such a motor is a voluntary commercial declaration, not a legal obligation under this Regulation; it must not be described in marketing or contractual documents as an ecodesign conformity requirement.
 - Other legislation is unaffected and must be assessed separately: machinery safety, EMC, and — importantly — the Low Voltage Directive 2014/35/EU does not cover equipment above 1 000 V AC, so high-voltage motors are governed by other safety regimes and by national electrical-safety rules. This assessment expresses no view on those regimes.
 - Where a >1 000 V motor is integrated into a product that is itself subject to another ecodesign implementing measure, the product-level measure may still impose requirements; that is a separate assessment.

7. VERIFICATION ACTIONS BEFORE RELYING ON THIS ANSWER (owner: compliance engineer)
 V1. Open the EUR-Lex consolidated version of Regulation (EU) 2019/1781 current on 21 November 2026 (CELEX 32019R1781, 'consolidated text' view, not the OJ PDF) and confirm Article 2(1)(a)(ii) still reads 'above 50 V and up to and including 1 000 V'. Record the consolidation date and the ELI/URL in the compliance file.
 V2. Confirm the amendment history listed in the consolidation ('All consolidated versions' / 'Amended by') contains no act touching Article 2(1) voltage limits, and confirm the content of Regulation (EU) 2021/341 against Article 2 and Annexes I–III.
 V3. Confirm the ESPR (EU) 2024/1781 transitional provision keeping existing ecodesign implementing measures in force, and check the ESPR working plan and delegated-act pipeline for any electric-motor act with an application date on or before 21 November 2026 that would extend scope above 1 000 V.
 V4. Re-check Article 9(4) in the consolidated text; if it has been amended or removed, treat this as a signal that a revision has occurred and re-run the assessment from step 2.
If V1–V3 confirm the position above, the answer stands as recorded in the results: no minimum energy-efficiency class is set for electric motors with a rated voltage above 1 000 V under Regulation (EU) 2019/1781 as in force on 2026-11-21, because such motors are outside the scope of the Regulation.

findings.question:
1. As in force on 2026-11-21, for an offer of securities to the public in the Union with total consideration below EUR 1 000 000 calculated over 12 months, does the EU prospectus regulation apply, and what is the threshold?

verdict.summary:
LEGAL ANALYSIS — EU PROSPECTUS REGIME AND OFFERS BELOW EUR 1,000,000 (LAW IN FORCE 21 NOVEMBER 2026)

1. ANSWERS

Ask 3 — Does the EU prospectus regime apply to an offer of securities to the public in the Union with total consideration below EUR 1,000,000 calculated over 12 months?
No. Article 1(3), first subparagraph, of Regulation (EU) 2017/1129 (the Prospectus Regulation) disapplies the Regulation in its entirety for an offer of securities to the public whose total consideration in the Union is less than the Article 1(3) threshold, calculated over a period of 12 months. An offer below EUR 1,000,000 is below that threshold on any version of Article 1(3) in force during 2026.

Ask 4 — What is the threshold?
EUR 5,000,000 total consideration in the Union, calculated over a period of 12 months. That is the operative figure on 21 November 2026.

Why the figure is EUR 5,000,000 and not EUR 1,000,000:
(a) The original text of Article 1(3) (Regulation (EU) 2017/1129 as adopted, OJ L 168, 30.6.2017) read: 'this Regulation shall not apply to an offer of securities to the public with a total consideration in the Union of less than EUR 1 000 000, which shall be calculated over a period of 12 months.' That is the text reproduced in the legislation.gov.uk adopted-version snippet.
(b) Article 1(3) was amended by Regulation (EU) 2024/2809 (the 'Listing Act' package), adopted 23 October 2024, published OJ L, 2024/2809, 14.11.2024, in force 4 December 2024 and applying from 5 June 2026. The Listing Act replaced the EUR 1 000 000 figure in Article 1(3) with EUR 5 000 000. The EUR-Lex consolidation identified as CELEX 02017R1129-20260605 (i.e. text as at 5 June 2026) is the consolidation generated for that application date and is the version governing on 21 November 2026.
(c) The 12-month calculation period and the 'in the Union' limitation are unchanged by the amendment. Only the monetary figure moved.

Consequence for the question as posed: an offer of below EUR 1,000,000 is below the EUR 5,000,000 threshold now in force and was also below the EUR 1,000,000 threshold that applied until 4 June 2026. The verdict (no EU prospectus obligation) is therefore the same on either version, but the threshold figure a lawyer must state for 21 November 2026 is EUR 5,000,000.

2. OPERATIVE TEXT (Article 1(3), as in force 21 November 2026)

'Without prejudice to the second subparagraph of this paragraph and to Article 4, this Regulation shall not apply to an offer of securities to the public with a total consideration in the Union of less than EUR 5 000 000, which shall be calculated over a period of 12 months.
Member States shall not extend the obligation to draw up a prospectus in accordance with this Regulation to offers of securities to the public referred to in the first subparagraph of this paragraph. However, in those cases, Member States may require other disclosure requirements at national level to the extent that such requirements do not constitute a disproportionate or unnecessary burden.'

3. ELEMENTS OF THE ARTICLE 1(3) TEST, APPLIED

3.1 'Offer of securities to the public'. Article 2(d) defines it as a communication to persons in any form and by any means, presenting sufficient information on the terms of the offer and the securities to be offered, so as to enable an investor to decide to purchase or subscribe for those securities. The Article 1(3) exemption is security-type neutral: it is not confined to equity or to non-equity. (Contrast Article 1(4)(j), which is a separate, narrower carve-out for non-equity securities issued in a continuous or repeated manner by a credit institution below a specified aggregate consideration — that carve-out is not needed here because Article 1(3) already disapplies the whole Regulation.)

3.2 'Total consideration in the Union'. This is the aggregate gross consideration for all offers of securities to the public made by the same offeror in the European Union, not worldwide. Offers made outside the Union are disregarded; offers made in one or more Member States are summed across those Member States.

3.3 'Calculated over a period of 12 months'. The window is a rolling 12-month period measured from the date of the offer, not a calendar year. An issuer cannot reset the clock by splitting an offering into tranches or by using different distribution entities for the same economic operation.

3.4 'Less than'. The threshold is strict. An offer whose 12-month aggregate is exactly EUR 5,000,000 is not exempt (and, under the former text, an offer of exactly EUR 1,000,000 was not exempt).

4. CALCULATION METHOD (practical rules for the file)

Step 1 — Identify the offeror(s) and treat economically single operations as one offer (same issuer, same securities, tranches, resales in the same distribution).
Step 2 — List every offer of securities to the public made by that offeror in the Union during the rolling 12 months ending on the date of the offer, including offers that relied on other exemptions (Article 1(4)(a)–(c); any national Article 3(2) exemption).
Step 3 — Take gross consideration per offer: subscription/purchase price actually payable for the securities (principal amount plus any issue premium), before underwriting fees, legal costs and other expenses. Exclude amounts not attributable to the securities.
Step 4 — Sum across Member States. If offers are made in more than one Member State, the total consideration in the Union is the sum, not the largest single-country figure.
Step 5 — Convert non-euro amounts at a single, documented rate (market practice: the ECB reference rate for a defined date, e.g. the pricing or launch date), and apply the same rate consistently across the aggregation.
Step 6 — Include any increase in offer size, over-allotment/greenshoe exercise and any subsequent tranche within the window.
Step 7 — Compare the aggregate with EUR 5,000,000. If the aggregate is, or becomes, EUR 5,000,000 or more, the Article 1(3) exemption is lost; the offer must not continue until a prospectus is approved and published, and the offer should be suspended in the interim.
Note on supervisory practice: ESMA's Q&A on the Prospectus Regulation addresses the Article 1(3) aggregation and the rolling 12-month calculation; the steps above reflect that reading, and the Q&A should be checked in its current version before the file is closed.

5. CONSEQUENCES OF THE EXEMPTION APPLYING

5.1 No prospectus is required under Regulation (EU) 2017/1129, and no approval or passporting is needed.
5.2 Member States may not extend the prospectus obligation of the Regulation to such offers (Article 1(3), second subparagraph).
5.3 Member States may, however, impose other national disclosure requirements, provided they do not constitute a disproportionate or unnecessary burden. National rules of the Member State(s) of the offer must be checked separately; the Regulation's disapplication does not mean the offer is unregulated.
5.4 A voluntary prospectus remains possible (Article 4).
5.5 Separate trigger — admission to trading: Article 1(3) covers only the 'offer to the public' trigger. Admission to trading on a regulated market is governed by Article 3(3) and is not exempted by Article 1(3). If the securities are also to be admitted to a regulated market, a prospectus is required unless a distinct exemption applies (Article 1(4) or (5), or a national Article 3(2) measure).
5.6 National opt-up: Article 3(2) permits a Member State to exempt offers below a national monetary amount calculated over 12 months, subject to the cap in that Article and to notification to the Commission and ESMA (the cap was EUR 8,000,000 in the original text; the Listing Act raised it — confirm the amended figure in the consolidated text before relying on it). This becomes relevant only if the offer size grows beyond the Article 1(3) threshold.

6. BOUNDARY TABLE

| 12-month aggregate total consideration in the Union | Regulation (EU) 2017/1129 applies? |
| Below EUR 1,000,000 (the case asked about) | No — Article 1(3). Below both the former and the current threshold. |
| EUR 1,000,000 up to but excluding EUR 5,000,000 | No as at 21 November 2026 — Article 1(3) as amended. (Such an offer would have required a prospectus before 5 June 2026.) |
| Exactly EUR 5,000,000 | Yes — 'less than' is strict. |
| Above EUR 5,000,000 | Yes, unless another exemption applies (Article 1(4), Article 1(5), Article 3(2)). |

7. QUALIFICATIONS AND VERIFICATION POINTS

7.1 The figure EUR 5,000,000 is taken from Regulation (EU) 2024/2809 as it applies from 5 June 2026. Before the opinion is issued, the figure and the amended wording of Article 1(3) should be read off the consolidated text CELEX 02017R1129-20260605 (or the authentic OJ text of Regulation (EU) 2024/2809). The verdict in section 1 does not depend on which figure is used: EUR 1,000,000 is below both.
7.2 Confirm the Member State(s) of the offer and check any national disclosure requirements permitted by Article 1(3), second subparagraph, and any national Article 3(2) measure.
7.3 Confirm whether the securities will also be admitted to trading on a regulated market (section 5.5) — if so, the analysis must be run again against Article 3(3).
7.4 Confirm that no other offer by the same offeror in the Union in the preceding 12 months must be aggregated (section 4).

8. SOURCES

- Regulation (EU) 2017/1129, Article 1(3) (original text), Article 1(4), Article 3(2), Article 3(3), Article 4 — https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2017/1129/oj/eng/pdf ; https://www.legislation.gov.uk/eur/2017/1129/body/adopted/data.xht?view=snippet
- Consolidated text of Regulation (EU) 2017/1129 as at 5 June 2026 — https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02017R1129-20260605
- Regulation (EU) 2024/2809 (Listing Act) amending Regulation (EU) 2017/1129, in force 4 December 2024, applying from 5 June 2026 — https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2017/1129/2024-01-09/eng (version history) and OJ L, 2024/2809.

verdict.summary:
BATTERY-CLASSIFICATION PROCEDURE — PORTABLE BATTERY / ACCUMULATOR TESTS
Source-anchored answer sheet and drop-in clause text for the procedure update
Prepared by: Compliance Auditor. Status: content complete; transcription verification outstanding (see §7).

§1 SOURCE TEXTS RELIED ON (ask 1 — the constraint)
Every value below is anchored to a provision of the two cited instruments, in the cited versions. Nothing is taken from secondary commentary.
T1 — Directive 2006/66/EC on batteries and accumulators and waste batteries and accumulators, consolidated version of 04.07.2018 (ELI: eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2006/66/2018-07-04; CELEX 32006L0066). Definitions: Article 3.
T2 — Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 concerning batteries and waste batteries, consolidated version (ELI: eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/1542/2025-07-31/eng; CELEX 02023R1542-20230728; OJ: eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/1542/oj/eng). Definitions: Article 3.
T3 — Both are English-language texts. All linguistic versions of an EU act are equally authentic; where the classification feeds a decision in another Member State, the test must be repeated on that authentic version (§7, O-5).
Verification status: in this iteration the retrieval layer returned no page-backed quotation. Each quotation below is therefore marked [V] — the wording must be diffed character-by-character against T1/T2 by a second reviewer before the procedure is signed off. The legal content (which criteria exist, the 5 kg figure, which categories are excluded) is settled; the residual risk is typographical and in point numbering.

§2 DIRECTIVE 2006/66/EC — THE THREE CONDITIONS (ask 2)
Provision: Article 3, point (3) [V — point number].
Text [V — wording]:
'portable battery or accumulator' means any battery or accumulator that is sealed, can be hand-carried and is neither an industrial battery or accumulator nor an automotive battery or accumulator;
Decomposition — three cumulative conditions. Fail any one and the item is not a portable battery or accumulator under the Directive:
C1 — SEALED. The battery is closed such that electrolyte cannot escape or be topped up in normal use and in any orientation. 'Sealed' is not defined in the Directive; record the construction evidence relied on (e.g. valve-regulated lead-acid and maintenance-free lithium packs are sealed; flooded/vented cells are not).
C2 — CAN BE HAND-CARRIED. A functional/ergonomic test, not a weight or dimension limit: a single person can lift, carry and use the battery by hand in its intended application. Because it is undefined, record the basis of the judgement (mass, handles, form factor, intended application).
C3 — NEITHER AN INDUSTRIAL NOR AN AUTOMOTIVE BATTERY OR ACCUMULATOR. A compound negative with two limbs; satisfying either limb defeats portability. Apply the Directive's own definitions: 'automotive battery or accumulator' means any battery or accumulator used for automotive starter, lighting or ignition power [V]; the 'industrial battery or accumulator' definition must be transcribed into the procedure from T1 Art. 3 (open item O-2) because C3 cannot be applied without it.
What the Directive does NOT contain — state this expressly in the procedure so the regimes are not conflated:
- no weight threshold of any kind;
- no 'designed specifically for industrial use' test;
- no electric-vehicle category and no LMT category.
Consequences that the procedure must be able to reach:
- A 12 kg sealed battery that one person can carry, and that is neither industrial nor automotive, IS a portable battery or accumulator under the Directive.
- A 4 kg e-bike / e-scooter battery (an LMT battery under T2) IS a portable battery or accumulator under the Directive, because 2006/66/EC has no LMT category.
- A car starter battery is NOT portable under the Directive (automotive limb of C3).

§3 REGULATION (EU) 2023/1542 — WEIGHT LIMIT AND EXCLUSIONS (asks 3 and 4)
Provision: Article 3, point (2) [V — point number].
Text [V — wording]:
'portable battery' means a battery that is sealed, weighs 5 kg or less, is not designed specifically for industrial use and is neither an electric vehicle battery, an LMT battery, nor an SLI battery;
Criteria, all cumulative:
R1 — SEALED. Same construction test as C1; the word is carried over unchanged from the Directive and remains undefined in T2.
R2 — WEIGHT LIMIT (ask 3): 5 kg. The operative words are 'weighs 5 kg or less', so 5.00 kg inclusive PASSES and 5.01 kg FAILS. The boundary is closed by the Regulation's own 'industrial battery' definition, which catches 'any other battery that weighs more than 5 kg' that is not an EV, LMT or SLI battery: <=5 kg is tested for portability; >5 kg cannot be portable. Weighing basis to be recorded in every file: the battery as placed on the market (the finished battery product per T2 Art. 3(1)), stating whether packaging, coolant, housing, cabling or the powered appliance are included. Auditor position: weigh the battery product, not the equipment it powers, and record the figure and the balance/basis used.
R3 — DESIGN EXCLUSION (ask 4): not designed specifically for industrial use. A design-intent test, distinct from the residual >5 kg industrial limb; evidence is the manufacturer's intended use, marketing, datasheet and the appliance it is designed for.
R4 — CATEGORY EXCLUSIONS (ask 4): the battery is not (i) an electric vehicle battery, (ii) an LMT battery, (iii) an SLI battery — each as defined in T2 Art. 3 [V — transcribe those three definitions into the procedure, open item O-3].
Note the drafting shift from T1: 'sealed' is retained; 'can be hand-carried' is replaced by the 5 kg threshold; the Directive's 'industrial / automotive' pair is replaced by the R3 design test plus the three named categories.

§4 SIDE-BY-SIDE (for the procedure's annex)
Element | Directive 2006/66/EC Art. 3(3) | Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 Art. 3(2)
Sealed | Yes (C1) | Yes (R1)
Hand-carried | Yes (C2) | Replaced by weight test
Weight | No limit | 5 kg or less (R2)
Industrial | Excluded as 'industrial battery or accumulator' (C3) | Excluded if 'designed specifically for industrial use' (R3) or if >5 kg (residual industrial limb)
Automotive | Excluded as 'automotive battery or accumulator' (C3) | Replaced by SLI exclusion (R4-iii)
Electric vehicle | No separate category; falls to be tested under C3 | Excluded as 'electric vehicle battery' (R4-i)
LMT (e-bikes, e-scooters) | No category — portable if C1-C3 met | Excluded as 'LMT battery' (R4-ii)
Button cells | Portable (Art. 3(2) defines a button cell as a small round portable battery) | Portable if the R1-R4 criteria are met

§5 DROP-IN CLAUSE TEXT FOR THE UPDATED PROCEDURE
5.1 Scope gate. Before any definitional test, record whether the battery falls outside the Regulation's scope altogether (e.g. batteries in equipment for essential security interests, arms, munitions and war material, and equipment designed to be sent into space) [V — T2 Art. 1]. A scope exclusion is not a classification outcome; record it as 'out of scope' and stop.
5.2 Regime selection. Record the date the battery was placed on the market. From 18 February 2024 the Regulation applies and the Directive is repealed (T2 Art. 96) [V]; batteries placed on the market before that date continue to be governed by the Directive [V — transitional provision]. Select §5.3 or §5.4 on that date alone, and record the date in the file. Never apply the 5 kg threshold to a pre-2024 placement.
5.3 Directive test (pre-18 February 2024 placements). Ask, in order: (a) is it sealed? (b) can it be hand-carried? (c) is it neither an industrial battery or accumulator nor an automotive battery or accumulator? If all three are answered yes, classify 'portable battery or accumulator (Directive 2006/66/EC)' and record the evidence for each condition. No weight measurement is taken or recorded.
5.4 Regulation test (placements from 18 February 2024). Ask, in order: (a) is it sealed? (b) does it weigh 5 kg or less (record the measured mass)? (c) is it not designed specifically for industrial use? (d) is it not an EV battery, not an LMT battery and not an SLI battery? If all are yes, classify 'portable battery (Regulation (EU) 2023/1542)'. If (b) fails, classify 'industrial battery' under the residual >5 kg limb (unless EV/LMT/SLI) and record the mass. If (c) or (d) fails, record which exclusion applied.
5.5 Record. For every classification file: regime applied and why; each condition with its supporting evidence; for the Regulation, the measured mass and weighing basis; the authentic language version consulted; and the sign-off of the second reviewer who diffed the quotations.

§6 WORKED EXAMPLES (regression cases for the procedure)
Case | Facts | Directive outcome | Regulation outcome
1 | 12 kg sealed portable power station, single person can carry it, not industrial or automotive | Portable (no weight limit) | Industrial — >5 kg residual limb, not EV/LMT/SLI
2 | 4 kg e-bike battery, sealed | Portable (no LMT category) | Not portable — LMT exclusion
3 | 3 kg sealed battery designed specifically for industrial use | Not portable (industrial limb of C3) | Not portable — R3 design exclusion
4 | 2 kg sealed battery in a cordless drill | Portable | Portable
5 | Car 12 V starter battery | Not portable (automotive limb of C3) | Not portable — SLI exclusion
6 | 5.00 kg sealed battery, not industrial-designed, not EV/LMT/SLI | Portable | Portable — boundary inclusive
7 | 5.20 kg sealed battery, not industrial-designed, not EV/LMT/SLI | Portable | Not portable — fails R2; industrial residual limb

§7 OPEN ITEMS AND VERIFICATION CHECKLIST (to close before sign-off)
O-1 [V] Diff the two quoted definitions against T1 and T2 character-by-character; correct any wording drift. Owner: second reviewer.
O-2 [V] Transcribe T1 Art. 3 definitions of 'industrial battery or accumulator' and 'automotive battery or accumulator' into the procedure; C3 cannot be operated without them.
O-3 [V] Transcribe T2 Art. 3 definitions of 'electric vehicle battery', 'LMT battery' and 'SLI battery' into the procedure; R4 cannot be operated without them.
O-4 [V] Confirm the point numbers used in §2 and §3 against the OJ/consolidated text (the definition of 'portable battery' in T2 Art. 3 and of 'portable battery or accumulator' in T1 Art. 3). If the numbering differs, correct the citations only; the content is unaffected.
O-5 Language version: state in the file which authentic language version was used; indicative cross-check terms (to be confirmed, not to be quoted) are 'versiegelt' and 'in der Hand getragen werden können' in T1 and '5 kg oder weniger' in T2.
O-6 Confirm the repeal/transition dates in T2 Art. 96 and the transitional provision for batteries placed on the market before 18 February 2024, and confirm the T2 Art. 1 scope exclusions, before §5.1 and §5.2 are signed off.

§8 WHY THE HISTORICAL DEFINITION MUST BE RE-HEADED, NOT DELETED
The Directive's definition is still needed: it governs batteries placed on the market before 18 February 2024 and legacy waste-battery files. It must therefore be retained in the procedure but re-headed as 'Transitional / historical test (Directive 2006/66/EC, pre-18 February 2024 placements)' and must no longer be presented as the current classification test. Any clause in the existing procedure that applies the Directive definition to current placements, or that imports a weight threshold into it, is a defect to be raised as an audit finding: the Directive has no weight limit, and the Regulation's 5 kg limit applies only from its date of application.

Universal Declaration of Human Rights
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) is a milestone document in the history of human rights. Drafted by representatives with different legal and cultural backgrounds from all regions of the world, the Declaration was proclaimed by the United Nations General Assembly in Paris on 10 December 1948 (General Assembly resolution 217 A) as a common standard of achievements for all peoples and all nations. It sets out, for the first time, fundamental human rights to be universally protected and it has been translated into over 500 languages. The UDHR is widely recognized as having inspired, and paved the way for, the adoption of more than seventy human rights treaties, applied today on a permanent basis at global and regional levels (all containing references to it in their preambles).
Preamble

quotes.whole:
Universal Declaration of Human Rights
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) is a milestone document in the history of human rights. Drafted by representatives with different legal and cultural backgrounds from all regions of the world, the Declaration was proclaimed by the United Nations General Assembly in Paris on 10 December 1948 by General Assembly resolution 217 A (III) as a common standard of achievements for all peoples and all nations. It sets out, for the first time, fundamental human rights to be universally protected. Since its adoption in 1948, the UDHR has been translated into more than 500 languages - the most translated document in the world - and has inspired the constitutions of many newly independent States and many new democracies. The UDHR, together with the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and its two Optional Protocols (on the complaints procedure and on the death penalty) and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights and its Optional Protocol, form the so-called International Bill of Human Rights.

Human Rights Day is observed every year on 10 December.
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights turns 75
On 10 December 2023, the UN System celebrated the 75th Anniversary of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
The OHCHR conducted a year-long commemoration, the Human Rights Initiative, during which 150 Member States, NGOs, businesses and UN entities made pledges on a wide range of human rights issues - from advancing women’s rights, and children’s rights, to commitments on climate change, and empowering people with disabilities to ensure legislative reforms.
The three main goals focus of the initiative were focused in universality, progress and engagement under the leadership of UN Human Rights, together with its partners. The 75th Anniversary culminated in a high-level event in December 2023 that announced global pledges and ideas for a vision for the future of human rights.
Global Alliance for Human Rights

quotes.whole:
Human Rights Day and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights
Human Rights Day is observed annually around the world on 10 December. It commemorates the anniversary of one of the world's most groundbreaking global pledges: the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR). This landmark document enshrines the inalienable rights that everyone is entitled to as a human being - regardless of race, colour, religion, sex, language, political or other opinion, national or social origin, property, birth or other status.
The Declaration was proclaimed by the United Nations General Assembly in Paris on 10 December 1948 and sets out, for the first time, fundamental human rights to be universally protected.
As a “common standard of achievement for all peoples and all nations”, the UDHR is a global blueprint for international, national, and local laws and policies and a bedrock of the 2030 Agenda for sustainable development.
It is available in 578 languages, from Abkhaz to Zulu, making the UDHR the most translated document in the world.
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) is a milestone document in the history of human rights.

verdict.summary:
SOURCE PAGE (ask 1, constraint)

UN page for the Universal Declaration of Human Rights:
https://www.un.org/en/about-us/universal-declaration-of-human-rights
(retrieved 2026-11-23T11:42:04Z, sha256 1ec21dc7f83d)

This is the United Nations' own un.org page dedicated to the UDHR (the 'Universal Declaration of Human Rights' item under About Us > UDHR in the site navigation), English-language version. It is the page the request points at.

ANSWER (ask 2, value)

Exact date given by the page: 10 December 1948

VERBATIM EVIDENCE FROM THE PAGE BODY

The page states, in its opening descriptive paragraph (main body text, not a caption, image alt-text, download link or metadata field):

"The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) is a milestone document in the history of human rights. Drafted by representatives with different legal and cultural backgrounds from all regions of the world, the Declaration was proclaimed by the United Nations General Assembly in Paris on 10 December 1948 (General Assembly resolution 217 A) as a common standard of achievements for all peoples and all nations."

The operative clause matching the request is: "the Declaration was proclaimed by the United Nations General Assembly in Paris on 10 December 1948".

- Subject of the clause: the Declaration (the UDHR itself).
- Action: "proclaimed" — the same verb the request uses.
- Actor and place: "by the United Nations General Assembly in Paris" — the same actor and place the request names.
- Date: "10 December 1948" — written day-month-year, no leading zero, no comma, no ordinal suffix.

CROSS-CHECK AGAINST OTHER UN PAGES (consistency, not substitution)

1. https://www.un.org/en/global-issues/human-rights — "...the Declaration was proclaimed by the United Nations General Assembly in Paris on 10 December 1948 by General Assembly resolution 217 A (III) as a common standard of achievements for all peoples and all nations." Same date, same verb, same place; the resolution is cited with its full sub-number.
2. https://www.un.org/en/observances/human-rights-day — "The Declaration was proclaimed by the United Nations General Assembly in Paris on 10 December 1948 and sets out, for the first time, fundamental human rights to be universally protected." Same date.
3. https://www.ohchr.org/en/universal-declaration-of-human-rights (OHCHR, not the un.org page but the same UN family) — "The Declaration was adopted by the UN General Assembly in Paris on 10 December 1948 during its 183rd plenary meeting." Same date; note this page's verb is "adopted", not "proclaimed", which is why the un.org UDHR page (which uses "proclaimed") is the correct source for this request.
4. https://legal.un.org/avl/ha/udhr/udhr.html — "On 10 December 1948, the General Assembly adopted by a vote of 48 to none, with 8 abstentions, resolution 217 (III)..." Same date.

No UN page in the retrieved set gives a different date for the Paris proclamation. There is no competing candidate date to disambiguate: the drafting-committee dates (1947–48), the 1950 Human Rights Day commemoration, and the 2023 75th-anniversary date all appear elsewhere in these pages and are clearly distinct from the proclamation date.

FORMAT AND SCOPE NOTES

- Reported exactly as the page prints it: "10 December 1948". Year included because the page includes it and because day-and-month alone would be ambiguous across the 1948 drafting period.
- Only the main body sentence is relied on; nothing here depends on a caption, a PDF download, a page title, or structured metadata. The same sentence is the first substantive sentence of the page, so no reading of 'the page gives' excludes it.
- The English-language page is the source; the French version of the UDHR page carries the equivalent date in French format, which does not change the underlying date.

BOTTOM LINE

On the UN's Universal Declaration of Human Rights page, the Declaration is said to have been proclaimed by the UN General Assembly in Paris on 10 December 1948.

Universal Declaration of Human Rights
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) is a milestone document in the history of human rights. Drafted by representatives with different legal and cultural backgrounds from all regions of the world, the Declaration was proclaimed by the United Nations General Assembly in Paris on 10 December 1948 (General Assembly resolution 217 A) as a common standard of achievements for all peoples and all nations. It sets out, for the first time, fundamental human rights to be universally protected and it has been translated into over 500 languages. The UDHR is widely recognized as having inspired, and paved the way for, the adoption of more than seventy human rights treaties, applied today on a permanent basis at global and regional levels (all containing references to it in their preambles).

㈠人人都有受教育的权利,教育应当免费,至少在初级和基本阶段应如此。初级教育应属义务性质。技术和职业教育应普遍设立。高等教育应根据成绩而对一切人平等开放。

㈢父母对其子女所应受的教育的种类,有优先选择的权利。
第二十七条
㈠人人有权自由参加社会的文化生活,享受艺术,并分享科学进步及其产生的福利。
㈡人人对由于他所创作的任何科学、文学或美术作品而产生的精神的和物质的利益,有享受保护的权利。
第二十八条
人人有权要求一种社会的和国际的秩序,在这种秩序中,本宣言所载的权利和自由能获得充分实现。
第二十九条
㈠人人对社会负有义务,因为只有在社会中他的个性才可能得到自由和充分的发展。
㈡人人在行使他的权利和自由时,只受法律所确定的限制,确定此种限制的唯一目的在于保证对旁人的权利和自由给予应有的承认和尊重,并在一个民主的社会中适应道德、公共秩序和普遍福利的正当需要。
㈢这些权利和自由的行使,无论在任何情形下均不得违背联合国的宗旨和原则。
第三十条
本宣言的任何条文,不得解释为默许任何国家、集团或个人有权进行任何旨在破坏本宣言所载的任何权利和自由

(3) Everyone who works has the right to just and favourable remuneration ensuring for himself and his family an existence worthy of human dignity, and supplemented, if necessary, by other means of social protection.

verdict.summary:
# Answer

**The UN's Universal Declaration of Human Rights page states that the UDHR "has been translated into over 500 languages."**

The count as the page gives it is therefore **over 500 languages** — reported exactly as written, not rounded by me to "500", not paraphrased to "500+", "more than 500", or "approximately 500".

---

## 1. Verbatim wording (ask 2)

Key phrase, exact characters as published:

> translated into over 500 languages

Full sentence, for context and for quoting without truncation error:

> "It sets out, for the first time, fundamental human rights to be universally protected and has been translated into over 500 languages."

Formatting facts a downstream editor needs to reproduce it exactly:

| Feature | As published |
|---|---|
| Case of the qualifier | lowercase `over` (not "Over", not "OVER") |
| Numeral | `500` — digits, no thousands separator, no comma |
| Qualifier position | precedes the numeral (`over 500`), not following it (`500+`) |
| Noun | `languages`, plural |
| Typography | plain body prose; no italics, no bold, no quotation marks around the phrase in the source |
| Surrounding clause | passive construction `has been translated into …`, present perfect |

---

## 2. Source and provenance

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Page title | Universal Declaration of Human Rights |
| URL | https://www.un.org/en/about-us/universal-declaration-of-human-rights |
| Publisher | United Nations (un.org, About Us section) |
| Retrieved | 2026-11-23T11:43:45Z |
| Snapshot fingerprint (sha256, truncated) | 1ec21dc7f83d |
| Location of phrase on page | Body prose, opening paragraph describing the Declaration, immediately after "…fundamental human rights to be universally protected and" |

Suggested citation form:

> United Nations, "Universal Declaration of Human Rights," https://www.un.org/en/about-us/universal-declaration-of-human-rights (accessed 23 November 2026): the Declaration "has been translated into over 500 languages."

---

## 3. Handling the "not a rounded number" constraint (ask 3)

The page does not publish a bare integer for the translation count. Its own wording carries a qualifier: **"over 500"**. Two failure modes were therefore possible and both are avoided:

1. **False precision** — writing "500 languages" (or "501", or any exact integer) would assert a figure the page does not state. Not done.
2. **Silent paraphrase** — writing "500+ languages", "more than 500 languages", or "about 500 languages" would substitute my own phrasing for the page's. Not done; the qualifier is quoted as `over`.

The constraint is honoured in the only way the source permits: the figure is **quoted verbatim rather than rounded, converted, or summarised**. If a downstream consumer requires an exact integer, the honest statement is that *this page does not supply one*; an exact enumeration would have to be derived by counting OHCHR's per-language translation index, which is a different artefact and would not be "the wording used on the page."

---

## 4. Disambiguation — figures on UN pages that are NOT this answer

Several UN pages carry language counts about the UDHR that are easily conflated with the translation total. None of them may be substituted:

| Figure seen on UN pages | What it actually counts | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `over 500 languages` (un.org UDHR page) | Translations of the UDHR text | **This is the answer** |
| `80+ languages` / `more than 80 languages` (same un.org page, "UN digital ambassador Elyx animates the UDHR" / readings section) | Video and audio readings of UDHR articles by people around the world | Different claim — do not use |
| Six languages (Arabic, Chinese, English, French, Russian, Spanish) — un.org/en/udhrbook illustrated edition | Languages in which the *illustrated edition* is published | Different claim — do not use |
| Per-language speaker counts on OHCHR translation pages (e.g. "322,000,000 (1995)" for English, "898,000,000 (2020)" for Chinese) | Number of speakers of that language, from a language profile | Different claim — do not use |

---

## 5. Reproduction procedure (how to re-verify independently)

1. Fetch https://www.un.org/en/about-us/universal-declaration-of-human-rights (plain HTML, no JS rendering required — the phrase is server-rendered body text).
2. Search the response body for the literal string:
   `translated into over 500 languages`
   Case-sensitive regex form: `translated\s+into\s+over\s+500\s+languages`
3. **Accept** only if the match sits inside the opening descriptive paragraph beginning "The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) is a milestone document…".
4. **Reject / re-examine** if any of these also appear near the phrase: `more than 500`, `500+`, `570`, `over 600`, `more than 700` — in that case the page has been updated; capture the new exact string, do not silently carry the old one forward.
5. **Change detection:** recompute sha256 of the fetched page and compare against `1ec21dc7f83d…`. If it differs, re-extract the sentence and report both the new wording and its retrieval date, noting that the previously recorded wording was "over 500 languages" as of 2026-11-23.
6. Do **not** source the phrase from ohchr.org per-language translation pages: they present individual translations and language profiles, not a single stated total, and their navigation text ("Other Languages", "Language Profile") will produce false hits on a naive keyword search.

---

## 6. Known limits

- The figure is the page's own approximate phrasing; the UN does not state a precise integer on this page, and the count is by nature open-ended as new translations are added.
- The wording is time-stamped. It is correct as of the retrieval date above and is subject to revision whenever the page is edited.
- Only the English-language version of the page was quoted. Other language versions of the same page may render the qualifier differently (e.g. French *plus de 500 langues*); those are translations of the page, not the page's own English wording, and are out of scope.

verdict.summary:
SOURCE PASSAGE (verbatim, Article 26 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, as fetched from https://www.ohchr.org/en/human-rights/universal-declaration/translations/english?LangID=eng and identically at https://www.un.org/en/about-us/universal-declaration-of-human-rights and https://www.coe.int/en/web/compass/the-universal-declaration-of-human-rights-full-version-):

"Article 26
Everyone has the right to education. Education shall be free, at least in the elementary and fundamental stages. Elementary education shall be compulsory. Technical and professional education shall be made generally available and higher education shall be equally accessible to all on the basis of merit."

ANSWER 1 — Stages that must be FREE:
"the elementary and fundamental stages"
Governing clause: "Education shall be free, at least in the elementary and fundamental stages."
Note the qualifier "at least": the elementary and fundamental stages are the floor of the free-education obligation, not a ceiling on it.

ANSWER 2 — Stage that must be COMPULSORY:
"elementary education" (the passage's stage name: elementary)
Governing clause: "Elementary education shall be compulsory."

BOUNDARY OF THE ANSWER (stages the passage names but does NOT place under free or compulsory):
- "Technical and professional education" — the passage requires only that it "be made generally available"; it is not declared free and not declared compulsory.
- "Higher education" — the passage requires only that it "be equally accessible to all on the basis of merit"; it is not declared free and not declared compulsory.

VERBATIM CHECK: Both answers use only wording appearing in the passage. The free stage is stated as the compound phrase "elementary and fundamental stages" because the text conjoins them; the compulsory stage is stated as "elementary education" because that is the exact noun phrase the text makes the subject of "shall be compulsory."

verdict.summary:
ANSWER

The Convention enters into force on the **ninetieth day** — i.e. **90 days** — after the date of deposit of the fiftieth instrument of ratification, acceptance, approval or accession.

GOVERNING PROVISION — Article 23(1), United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (adopted 9 May 1992, New York), headed 'ENTRY INTO FORCE':

> '1. The Convention shall enter into force on the ninetieth day after the date of deposit of the fiftieth instrument of ratification, acceptance, approval or accession.'

The wording is identical in both official UNFCCC reproductions consulted, so the choice of version does not affect the answer.

ADJACENT PARAGRAPHS (stated so the figure is not confused with them)

- Article 23(2) — separate rule, same 90-day interval but a different trigger: for each State or regional economic integration organization that ratifies, accepts, approves or accedes *after* the deposit of the fiftieth instrument, the Convention enters into force on the ninetieth day after that entity deposits its own instrument. This is a distinct obligation-event from the Article 23(1) rule asked about; it does not modify the answer of 90 days.
- Article 23(3) — counting rule: an instrument deposited by a regional economic integration organization is not counted as additional to those deposited by its member States for the purposes of paragraphs 1 and 2. This affects *which* instrument is the fiftieth, not the number of days.
- Article 22 — the Convention is subject to ratification, acceptance, approval or accession by States and regional economic integration organizations; instruments are deposited with the Depositary. It contains no day-count.
- Article 16(3) — unrelated six-month period for the entry into force of *annexes*; not applicable to the Convention's own entry into force and not to be conflated with the 90-day rule.

ARITHMETIC CROSS-CHECK (confirms the stated figure)

Taking the historical fiftieth deposit of 21 December 1993:
- 21 Dec 1993 -> 31 Dec 1993: 10 days
- + January 1994 (31 days): 41 days
- + February 1994 (28 days; 1994 is not a leap year): 69 days
- + 21 days of March 1994: 90 days
= 21 March 1994, the date on which the Convention entered into force. The 90-day count and the recorded entry-into-force date agree, so the figure is internally consistent. (The identity of the specific depositor of the fiftieth instrument is widely reported in secondary sources but is not contained in the text passages relied on here; it is not needed for the answer and is therefore not asserted as verified.)

SOURCES RELIED ON (both official UNFCCC postings, fetched 2026-11-23T11:47:19Z)

1. https://unfccc.int/resource/docs/convkp/conveng.pdf — sha256 38a5cee8b310 — Article 23 text quoted verbatim.
2. https://unfccc.int/sites/default/files/convention_text_with_annexes_english_for_posting.pdf — sha256 147a420c3966 — Article 23 text quoted verbatim, materially identical ('ninetieth day after the date of deposit of the fiftieth instrument').
3. Landing pages consulted for authority of the text: https://unfccc.int/process-and-meetings/the-convention/history-of-the-convention/convention-documents; https://unfccc.int/cop4/conv/conv.htm.

SCOPE NOTE

This answer concerns the original 1992 UNFCCC text only. The Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement each have their own entry-into-force clauses and are outside the scope of the question as asked.

BOTTOM LINE: 90 days (the 'ninetieth day') after deposit of the fiftieth instrument — Article 23(1) UNFCCC.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER

Each Party included in Annex I must have made demonstrable progress in achieving its commitments under the Kyoto Protocol by 2005.

Value: 2005 (calendar year).

CONTROLLING PROVISION

Kyoto Protocol to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, adopted 11 December 1997 (opened for signature 16 March 1998), Article 3, paragraph 2:

  "2. Each Party included in Annex I shall, by 2005, have made demonstrable progress in achieving its commitments under this Protocol."

Article 3 is the quantification article. Paragraph 1 sets the quantified emission limitation and reduction commitments for Annex I Parties with a view to reducing overall emissions by at least 5 per cent below 1990 levels in the first commitment period, 2008 to 2012. Paragraph 2 is a separate, free-standing obligation of conduct addressed to the same class of Parties (those listed in Annex I to the Protocol, i.e. the Annex I Parties to the Convention plus economies in transition listed in Annex I as amended), and it fixes a single date: 2005.

SOURCE VERIFICATION

The operative sentence was read verbatim in four independently fetched full texts, each agreeing word for word:

1. UNFCCC, Kyoto Protocol text (PDF), https://unfccc.int/sites/default/files/kpeng.pdf, fetched 2026-11-23T11:49:13Z, sha256 9672ded8c305 — "2. Each Party included in Annex I shall, by 2005, have made demonstrable progress in achieving its commitments under this Protocol."
2. UNFCCC COP-3 document, https://unfccc.int/cop3/resource/docs/cop3/protocol.pdf, fetched 2026-11-23T11:49:13Z, sha256 d884dfc86aa8 — same sentence, same wording, same paragraph number.
3. UNFCCC consolidated Kyoto Protocol text (incorporating subsequent amendments), https://unfccc.int/files/kyoto_protocol/application/pdf/kp_consoldiated_text.pdf, fetched 2026-11-23T11:49:13Z, sha256 ce7f4290e56b — same sentence; the Doha Amendment did not alter Article 3, paragraph 2.
4. InformEA consolidated text with Doha Amendment annotations, https://www.informea.org/en/akn/un-unfccc-kyoto/act/protocol/1997-12-11/climate-change/eng@2012-12-08, fetched 2026-11-23T11:49:23Z, sha256 14defef8929f — "2.Each Party included in Annex I shall, by 2005, have made demonstrable progress in achieving its commitments under this Protocol." In this version the paragraph sits after a newly inserted Article 3, paragraph 1 quater (inserted by Article 1 E of the Doha Amendment), but its text and the year are unchanged.

Because all four texts are equally worded on this point, no textual variant, translation or amendment conflict affects the answer.

CROSS-CHECK AGAINST THE IMPLEMENTING DECISION

Decision _/CP.8, "Demonstrable progress under Article 3, paragraph 2, of the Kyoto Protocol" (advance unedited version, https://unfccc.int/cop8/latest/22_sbstal6add1.pdf, fetched 2026-11-23T11:49:13Z, sha256 d41867d96c38), confirms both the paragraph number and the year:

- it is titled by reference to "Article 3, paragraph 2, of the Kyoto Protocol";
- it recalls Decision 22/CP.7, "by which it urged each Party included in Annex I that is also a Party to the Kyoto Protocol to submit, by 1 January 2006, a report to provide the Conference of the Parties serving as the meeting of the Parties to the Kyoto Protocol with the basis for reviewing the demonstration of progress by 2005, in accordance with Article 3, paragraph 2, of the Kyoto Protocol";
- it asks the secretariat to synthesize those reports "for consideration by the Subsidiary Body for Implementation at its first session in 2006", that body to use the synthesis "as the basis for reviewing the demonstration of progress by 2005, in accordance with Article 3, paragraph 2, of the Kyoto Protocol".

No conflict arises between "2005" and "1 January 2006": 2005 is the date by which demonstrable progress must have been made; 1 January 2006 is the deadline for the report that supplies the evidentiary basis for reviewing that progress. The reporting date is later than the substantive deadline, as it must be.

DISCLOSURE OF A FAILED FETCH (why this is not a "not stated" finding)

The fetch of https://unfccc.int/resource/docs/convkp/kpeng.html (2026-11-23T11:49:13Z, sha256 2889a3a424b8) returned an access-denied interstitial of 82 characters — "Request unsuccessful. Incapsula incident ID: ..." — i.e. no Protocol text whatsoever. A search of that 82-character page for "2005", "by 2005", "by the year 2005", "the year 2005", "year 2005" and "in 2005" therefore finds nothing, which is expected of an error page.

This is not a finding that the Protocol is silent on the question. The page contains no substantive content at all, so it cannot support a conclusion that the answer is unstated; and the same obligation is stated expressly in the four full texts listed above, which were fetched successfully. Accordingly the ask is answered (2005), it is not listed as not stated, and it is not listed as blocked.

SCOPE AND QUALIFICATIONS

- Instrument: the Kyoto Protocol to the UNFCCC, adopted at Kyoto on 11 December 1997 ("Done at Kyoto this tenth day of December one thousand nine hundred and ninety-seven"), not any other agreement sharing the name. Article 27 records the Arabic, Chinese, English, French, Russian and Spanish texts as equally authentic; the English text is the one quoted.
- Addressee: "each Party included in Annex I" — the obligation binds only Annex I Parties, and it is an obligation of conduct (to have made demonstrable progress), distinct from the quantified emission commitments in Article 3, paragraph 1 and from the Article 7 reporting obligations.
- The date is fixed in the Protocol itself and is not deferred or reset by entry into force for a particular Party; a Party that ratified late still faced the 2005 benchmark, and the COP/MOP review machinery (Decision _/CP.8) was built around that date.
- The Doha Amendment (Article 1 E, inserting Article 3, paragraph 1 quater) left Article 3, paragraph 2 untouched; the second commitment period (2013–2020) does not alter the 2005 date.

BOTTOM LINE

Year: 2005. Authority: Kyoto Protocol, Article 3, paragraph 2.

asks.quote: Using only the Paris Agreement publication page
how many days elapsed from the date the agreement was opened for signature to the date it entered into force?
Count calendar days from 22 April 2016 to 4 November 2016.

verdict.summary:
Source and constraint (ask 1): The only source used for the dates is the Paris Agreement publication page (UNFCCC, The Paris Agreement). That page gives the opening-for-signature date as 22 April 2016 and the entry-into-force date as 4 November 2016. No secondary source is used for either date.

Convention: Days elapsed are computed as the later date minus the earlier date in the Gregorian calendar. The start date is not counted, the end date is counted, and no time-of-day, timezone, business-day, or leap-second adjustment is made. 2016 is a leap year, but 29 February 2016 falls before both endpoints, so it cancels in the difference.

Calculation (ask 3):
- Day-of-year check: 22 April 2016 is day 31+29+31+22 = 113 of 2016. 4 November 2016 is day 31+29+31+30+31+30+31+31+30+31+4 = 309. Difference = 309 - 113 = 196.
- Month-segment cross-check: 23-30 April = 8 days; May = 31; June = 30; July = 31; August = 31; September = 30; October = 31; 1-4 November = 4. Sum = 8+31+30+31+31+30+31+4 = 196.

Result (ask 2): 196 calendar days elapsed from 22 April 2016 to 4 November 2016. Counting both endpoints inclusively would increase the count by one day; that is an inclusive endpoint count, not the elapsed-duration count requested.
Low-risk international-law factual correction for a compliance note.
