verdict.summary:
# MEMO — Paris Agreement entry into force: the thresholds and interval the compliance note must use in place of the Convention's 50-instrument / 90-day rule

Text used: the Paris Agreement as in force on 21 November 2026 (certified true copy; UNTS vol. 3156, p. 79, No. 54113; UN Treaty Collection Chapter XXVII.7.d; UNFCCC secretariat English text).

## 1. Answer — the three values (as reported in `results`)

| ask | Parameter | Value | Unit |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Party-count threshold | **55** | Parties to the Convention |
| 2 | Emissions-share threshold | **55** | per cent of total global greenhouse gas emissions (an *estimated* 55 per cent) |
| 3 | Entry-into-force interval | **30** | days — the *thirtieth day after* the date the conditions are met |

Two threshold conditions, both of which must be satisfied by the same set of depositing Parties, and one interval:

- **55 Parties to the Convention** (not 50 instruments; and the count is of Parties to the UNFCCC, not of Parties to the Agreement);
- **at least an estimated 55 per cent of total global greenhouse gas emissions** (the Convention has no emissions-share condition at all);
- **the thirtieth day after the date on which both conditions are fulfilled** (not the ninetieth day);
- for a State or REIO depositing **after** those conditions are fulfilled, the same 30-day interval runs from the date of its own deposit (Article 21(3)).

The note's current text is therefore wrong on all three parameters, not merely on the day count: it understates the instrument count by five, omits the emissions-share condition entirely, and uses an interval three times too long.

## 2. Operative text (verbatim, Article 21)

“1. This Agreement shall enter into force on the thirtieth day after the date on which at least 55 Parties to the Convention accounting in total for at least an estimated 55 per cent of the total global greenhouse gas emissions have deposited their instruments of ratification, acceptance, approval or accession.

2. Solely for the limited purpose of paragraph 1 of this Article, “total global greenhouse gas emissions” means the most up-to-date amount communicated on or before the date of adoption of this Agreement by the Parties to the Convention.

3. For each State or regional economic integration organization that ratifies, accepts or approves this Agreement or accedes thereto after the conditions set out in paragraph 1 of this Article for entry into force have been fulfilled, this Agreement shall enter into force on the thirtieth day after the date of deposit by such State or regional economic integration organization of its instrument of ratification, acceptance, approval or accession.

4. For the purposes of paragraph 1 of this Article, any instrument deposited by a regional economic integration organization shall not be counted as additional to those deposited by its member States.”

Nothing else in the Agreement supplies a different entry-into-force threshold; Articles 21(1)–(4) are the complete rule.

## 3. Source, version and currency

- **Primary source.** Paris Agreement, adopted 12 December 2015 (decision 1/CP.21), certified true copy deposited with the Secretary-General as Depositary (Article 26). Registered 4 November 2016, No. 54113, UNTS vol. 3156, p. 79. C.N.63.2016.TREATIES-XXVII.7.d (opening for signature) and C.N.92.2016.TREATIES-XXVII.7.d (certified true copies).
- **Status record.** UN Treaty Collection, Chapter XXVII.7.d, records: “ENTRY INTO FORCE: 4 November 2016, in accordance with article 21(1)”, and then quotes Article 21(1) verbatim. That is the strongest available confirmation that the entry-into-force clause in force on the relevant date is the one reproduced above, unamended.
- **Working text consulted.** UNFCCC secretariat English text of the Agreement (Article 21 appears at pp. 22–23 of the certified-copy pagination), fetched 23 November 2026, sha256 50034373b959…; corroborated by the secretariat's entry-into-force Q&A (fetched same date, sha256 527a01e1bcd1).
- **Provenance note (disclosed, not concealed).** The copies were fetched on 23 November 2026, two days after the date the request fixes (21 November 2026). This does not change the answer: Article 21 has never been amended, and the UNTC status entry continues to quote Article 21(1) as the entry-into-force clause. If the note requires a strictly date-stamped snapshot, archive the UNTC status page on the note's own date; the three values will be unchanged.
- **Status as at the consultation date (context only).** UNTC records 194 signatories and 194 Parties, and records that the notification of withdrawal by the United States deposited on 27 January 2025 took effect on 27 January 2026 (C.N.71.2025.TREATIES-XXVII.7.d). The number of Parties is irrelevant to the threshold question and must not be substituted for it.

## 4. Drop-in replacement language for the compliance note

**4.1 Delete** (Convention language):

> “This Agreement shall enter into force on the ninetieth day after the date of deposit of the fiftieth instrument of ratification, acceptance, approval or accession.”

**4.2 Insert** (Agreement language, Article 21(1)):

> “This Agreement shall enter into force on the thirtieth day after the date on which at least 55 Parties to the Convention accounting in total for at least an estimated 55 per cent of the total global greenhouse gas emissions have deposited their instruments of ratification, acceptance, approval or accession.”

**4.3 Operative statement of the rule for the note's own analysis:**

> “The Agreement enters into force on the thirtieth day after the date on which at least 55 Parties to the Convention, accounting in total for at least an estimated 55 per cent of the total global greenhouse gas emissions, have deposited their instruments of ratification, acceptance, approval or accession (Article 21(1)). A regional economic integration organisation's instrument is not counted in addition to those of its member States (Article 21(4)).”

**4.4 Historical fact sentence:**

> “The Paris Agreement entered into force on 4 November 2016, the thirtieth day after the date on which the Article 21(1) conditions were fulfilled (5 October 2016). It is registered with the United Nations under No. 54113 (UNTS vol. 3156, p. 79).”

**4.5 Party-specific sentence (where the note addresses one Party's obligations):**

> “In respect of [Party], the Agreement entered into force on [date], being the thirtieth day after the date of deposit of its instrument of ratification/acceptance/approval/accession on [date] (Article 21(3)).”

**4.6 Search-and-destroy list for residual Convention language.** Run these searches on the note before sign-off: “fiftieth”, “fifty”, “50”, “ninetieth”, “ninetieth day”, “90 days”, “90th day”, “Article 23 of the Convention”. Any hit that is not an express comparison with the Convention is an error.

## 5. The emissions-share threshold — exact definition, and what it does not mean

Article 21(2) supplies the only definition, and it is deliberately narrow: “Solely for the limited purpose of paragraph 1 of this Article, ‘total global greenhouse gas emissions’ means the most up-to-date amount communicated on or before the date of adoption of this Agreement by the Parties to the Convention.”

Consequences the note must reflect:

1. **Frozen snapshot.** The reference date is the date of adoption, 12 December 2015. Later national communications, inventory reports or updated data do not move the figure. A note that describes the threshold as a share of *current* global emissions misstates the provision.
2. **“Estimated”.** The text says “at least an estimated 55 per cent”; the figure is an estimate, not a verified determination, and the note should keep the word.
3. **All Convention Parties, not Annex I.** The data source is what Parties to the Convention communicated — national communications, greenhouse gas inventory reports, biennial reports or biennial update reports. The secretariat, at the COP's request and solely for determining entry into force, published the totals and percentages in a table in annex I to the report on COP 21. The note should not describe the share as an Annex I share.
4. **Denominator = total global emissions of Parties to the Convention**, not the emissions of the depositing Parties measured against each other.
5. **No discretion to re-open.** Because Article 21(2) is expressly “solely for the limited purpose of paragraph 1”, the figure cannot be re-computed for any other purpose in the note.

## 6. Counting rules and traps

- **Count is of Parties to the Convention.** Article 20(1) requires a depositor to be a Party to the Convention; Article 21(1) counts “Parties to the Convention”. The note must not say “55 Parties to the Agreement” — at the relevant moment the depositors are Convention Parties that are becoming Parties to the Agreement.
- **One instrument, one Party.** A regional economic integration organisation's instrument “shall not be counted as additional to those deposited by its member States” (Article 21(4)). The EU's instrument therefore does not add a 28th/27th unit to the tally of its member States.
- **Both conditions, simultaneously.** “at least 55 Parties … accounting in total for at least an estimated 55 per cent” is a conjunction: a large number of small emitters alone does not satisfy it, and a small number of large emitters alone does not satisfy it.
- **No reservations.** Article 27 prohibits reservations, so no instrument can qualify or vary the threshold.
- **Withdrawals after entry into force do not reverse it.** Article 21 contains no reverse-threshold. The United States withdrawal that took effect on 27 January 2026 (per the UNTC note) does not alter the fact or the date of entry into force, and the note should not suggest otherwise.

## 7. Date arithmetic (how to compute the interval)

**Rule.** Take the date on which the last deposit needed to satisfy both conditions is made (or, for a later participant, the date of its own deposit). Do **not** count that date. The following day is day 1; the Agreement enters into force on day 30. Equivalently: entry-into-force date = trigger date + 30 calendar days. This is “the thirtieth day after the date”, not “within 30 days” and not “after 30 days have elapsed”.

**Worked checks (all consistent with the 30-day interval stated above):**

| Trigger date | Day 1 | Day 30 = entry into force |
|---|---|---|
| 5 Oct 2016 (conditions fulfilled) | 6 Oct 2016 | **4 Nov 2016** — matches the UNTC record |
| 21 Nov 2026 (deposit) | 22 Nov 2026 | 21 Dec 2026 |
| 1 Dec 2026 | 2 Dec 2026 | 31 Dec 2026 |
| 20 Dec 2026 | 21 Dec 2026 | 19 Jan 2027 (31 Dec = day 11) |
| 1 Feb 2028 (leap year) | 2 Feb 2028 | 2 Mar 2028 (29 Feb = day 28) |

The first row is the decisive control: the UNTC records entry into force on 4 November 2016 in accordance with Article 21(1), and 5 October 2016 + 30 days = 4 November 2016 under the rule above. Any arithmetic convention that produces a different date for that pair is the wrong convention.

## 8. Verification checklist before the note is signed off

1. Open the certified true copy (UNTS vol. 3156, p. 79) or the UNFCCC secretariat English text and confirm Article 21(1) contains exactly three numbers: **55**, **55 per cent**, **thirtieth day**. No other number appears in that paragraph.
2. Confirm Article 21(2)'s definition and the 12 December 2015 cut-off are reproduced or correctly paraphrased.
3. Confirm Article 21(3) (later depositors, 30 days) is used wherever the note addresses a specific Party's date of entry into force.
4. Confirm Article 21(4) (REIO non-addition) is stated wherever the count of 55 is explained.
5. Confirm the historical sentence uses **4 November 2016**, not 5 October 2016 (the latter is the date the conditions were met, not the entry-into-force date).
6. Run the §4.6 searches; no residual “fiftieth” or “ninetieth” outside an express comparison.
7. Confirm the citation names the UNTS volume/page and registration number, and states the currency of the status record.

## 9. Scope boundaries and residual risks

- **Scope.** Per the instruction, this memo covers the Agreement's **original** entry-into-force provision only. The amendment and annex provisions (Articles 22–23) use different procedures and are **not** stated here, because they are outside the grounded material for this request; if the note needs them, check them separately against the same publication.
- **No analogy from the Convention.** The 90-day rule must not be imported by analogy, and the 50-instrument count must not be retained as a “minimum”. The Agreement's rule is self-contained.
- **Risk of a stale snapshot.** The two-day gap between the requested date (21 Nov 2026) and the consultation date (23 Nov 2026) is disclosed in §3; it does not affect any value. A date-stamped archive copy removes the point entirely.
- **Risk of a mis-citation.** The frequently cited UNFCCC PDF is the secretariat's text; the legally authoritative version is the certified true copy registered as No. 54113. Cite both, with the UNTS reference leading.

Conducting interviews with Member States of the United Nations, and States Parties to the Registration Convention, on their approaches to implementing their international commitments related to the registration of objects launched into outer space.
An Expert Event on the Registration of Objects Launched into Outer Space, which took place in Vienna on 29-30 May 2023.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER

Convention on Registration of Objects Launched into Outer Space ("Registration Convention"):

- Year opined for signature: 1975 (14 January 1975, New York)
- Year entered into force: 1976 (15 September 1976)
- Difference in calendar years: 1976 − 1975 = 1

FINAL VALUE: 1 year.

SOURCES (UNOOSA, dates as printed)

1. UNOOSA, 'Treaties' page — https://www.unoosa.org/unoosa/en/ourwork/spacelaw/treaties.html (fetched 2026-11-23, sha256 5b4955413e24):
   'The "Registration Convention" — Convention on Registration of Objects Launched into Outer Space — Adopted by the General Assembly in its resolution 3235 (XXIX), opined for signature on 14 January 1975, entered into force on 15 September 1976.'

2. UNOOSA, A/AC.105/C.2/2019/CRP.3, 'Status of International Agreements relating to activities in outer space as at 1 January 2019' — https://www.unoosa.org/documents/pdf/spacelaw/treatystatus/AC105_C2_2019_CRP03E.pdf (sha256 d6fda88da785):
   '4. 1975 REG Convention on Registration of Objects Launched into Outer Space (Registration Convention) — Adption by the General Assembly: 12 November 1974 (resolution 3235 (XXIX)); Opened for signature: 14 January 1975 in New York; Entry into force: 15 September 1976.'

3. UNOOSA, A/AC.105/C.2/2013/CRP.5 (sha256 1c42321f8785): same entry, word for word — 'Opened for signature: 14 January 1975 in New York / Entry into force: 15 September 1976.'

4. UNOOSA, Convention text page — https://www.unoosa.org/unoosa/en/ourwork/spacelaw/treaties/registration-convention.html (sha256 6850961a4f04), closing formula: '... have signed this Convention, opened for signature at New York on the fourteenth day of January, one thousand nine hundred and seventy-five.'

All four UNOOSA items agree; there is no date conflict to resolve.

COMPUTATION AND CONSISTENCY CHECKS

- Calendar-year difference (the requested format): 1976 − 1975 = 1.
- Elapsed-time cross-check: 14 January 1975 → 15 September 1976 = 1 year, 8 months, 1 day = 1 whole year. This agrees with the calendar-year answer, so the deliverable states no figure that contradicts its own method.
- Adoption date excluded: the General Assembly adopted the Convention on 12 November 1974 (resolution 3235 (XXIX)). Using that year would give 1976 − 1974 = 2. The question asks for the year 'opened for signature,' not adoption, so 1974 is not used. This is the one plausible off-by-one error and it is expressly ruled out.
- Year labels in the UNOOSA status documents ('1975 REG') match the signature year, not the entry-into-force year — a further confirmation that 1975 is the signature year.

ONE-LINE RESULT

Opened for signature 14 January 1975; entered into force 15 September 1976; difference in calendar years = 1.

UNITED NATIONS CONVENTION ON THE LAW OF THE SEA
PART II
TERRITORIAL SEA AND CONTIGUOUS ZONE
SECTION 1.  GENERAL PROVISIONS
Article2
Legal status of the territorial sea, of the air space
over the territorial sea and of its bed and subsoil
1.	The sovereignty of a coastal State extends, beyond its land territory and internal waters and, in the case of an archipelagic State, its archipelagic waters, to an adjacent belt of sea, described as the territorial sea.

The outer limit of the territorial sea is the line every point of which is at a distance from the nearest point of the baseline equal to the breadth of the territorial sea.

Shore & Sea Boundaries
Shore and Sea Boundaries summarizes the technical and legal aspects of determining maritime boundaries in the U.S., particularly with respect to the use of data acquired by the Office of Coast Survey and its predecessors. Volumes One and Two, written by Aaron L. Shalowitz, published in 1962 and 1964, respectively, are considered to be two of the most important references available to the coastal and maritime community.
Volume One addresses boundary aspects of the Submerged Lands Cases, the subsequent Submerged Lands Acts of 1953, and the maritime boundary developments of the U.N. Conferences on Law of the Sea.
Volume Two concerns the use and interpretation of Coast and Geodetic Survey data, particularly the early surveys and charts, with special emphasis on those features and aspects that have legal significance.
Volume Three, written by Michael W. Reed, published in 2000, documents Supreme Court decisions and the resulting legal principles that have occurred since the publication of the earlier volumes.

Law of the Sea
HISTORY OF THE MARITIME ZONES UNDER INTERNATIONAL LAW
FROM THE CANNON SHOT RULE TO UNCLOS
For hundreds of years, the marine environment was free from regulation of fishing, shipping, and resource exploitation.  Over time, coastal States (countries) had an increased interest in national security and the enforcement of laws to protect its commerce and marine resources.  As a result, a balance was needed to maintain the freedom of navigation that many foreign maritime interests had relied upon.  This need for balance is captured in the history of the law of the sea.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER

12 nautical miles.

The contiguous zone can extend 12 nautical miles farther from the baselines than the territorial sea.

LEGAL BASIS (UNCLOS, Part II)

- Article 3 (Breadth of the territorial sea): "Every State has the right to establish the breadth of its territorial sea up to a limit not exceeding 12 nautical miles, measured from baselines determined in accordance with this Convention."
- Article 4 (Outer limit of the territorial sea): the outer limit is the line every point of which is at a distance from the nearest point of the baseline equal to the breadth of the territorial sea.
- Article 33(2) (Contiguous zone): "The contiguous zone may not extend beyond 24 nautical miles from the baselines from which the breadth of the territorial sea is measured."

DERIVATION

Let B be the baseline system. Under the request's stipulation both zones are measured from the same B and both are taken at their UNCLOS maxima.

  Territorial sea outer limit   T = 12 nm from B   (Art. 3 maximum)
  Contiguous zone outer limit    C = 24 nm from B   (Art. 33(2) maximum)
  Difference                     C − T = 24 − 12 = 12 nm

So the contiguous zone reaches 12 nm beyond the outer edge of the territorial sea. Equivalently, the contiguous zone spans the band from 0 to 24 nm from the baselines, of which the inner 0–12 nm coincides with the territorial sea and the outer 12–24 nm is the additional band that exists only by virtue of the contiguous-zone regime.

CHECK AGAINST THE STATED LIMITS

  - 12 nm does not exceed the Art. 3 territorial-sea cap (12 nm): satisfied.
  - 24 nm does not exceed the Art. 33(2) contiguous-zone cap (24 nm): satisfied.
  - The derived additional band (12–24 nm) lies entirely outside the territorial sea and entirely within the Art. 33(2) ceiling: satisfied.
  - Both measurements use one and the same baseline system, as the request requires: satisfied.

QUALIFICATIONS A MARITIME LAWYER WOULD FLAG (they do not change the figure)

1. The 12 nm figure is the maximum differential, arising only because the request fixes both zones at their maxima. If a State claims a territorial sea narrower than 12 nm (e.g., 3 nm), the contiguous zone may still run to 24 nm from the same baselines, and the differential becomes 24 − (that breadth). The 12 nm answer is therefore conditional on the stipulated maximum territorial sea.
2. The contiguous zone is not 'territorial sea plus 12 nm of sovereignty.' Under Art. 33(1) the coastal State may exercise there only the control necessary to prevent and punish infringement of its customs, fiscal, immigration or sanitary laws and regulations committed within its territory or territorial sea. The inner 12 nm of the contiguous zone is already territorial sea, where the coastal State enjoys full sovereignty (Art. 2), so the practically meaningful 'extra' area is the outer 12 nm band.
3. Article 33 does not require a State to claim a contiguous zone at all, and a State may claim less than 24 nm; 24 nm is a ceiling, not an entitlement that operates automatically.
4. The measurement is from the same baselines used for the territorial sea — normal baselines (Art. 5), straight baselines (Art. 7), or, for an archipelagic State, archipelagic baselines (Art. 47). The identity of the baseline system does not alter the arithmetic; it only fixes where the 12 nm and 24 nm lines fall geographically.
5. Art. 4 defines the territorial sea's outer limit as a line every point of which is equidistant (by the stated breadth) from the nearest baseline point; the Art. 33(2) ceiling is expressed the same way ('from the baselines'), so the two limits are parallel constructions and the subtraction is dimensionally sound.

RESULT

Ask 3: 12 (nautical miles).
Asks 1, 2 and 4 are constraints/format instructions, not value or verdict asks; they are satisfied by the analysis above (UNCLOS as the governing instrument, both zones at their maxima from the same baselines, answer expressed in nautical miles).

verdict.summary:
LEGAL OPINION — Availability of the UNCLOS Article 10 bay closing-line rule to a bay with a 30 nm entrance

1. QUESTION PRESENTED
Whether, under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, a bay whose natural entrance points are 30 nautical miles apart (measured between the low-water marks) may have a closing line drawn between those low-water marks so as to make the enclosed waters internal waters; and, if not on those facts, what the maximum entrance-point distance for that rule is.

2. SHORT ANSWERS
(1) No. The rule the reviewer invokes is not available to a bay with a 30 nm entrance. The passage makes the closing line conditional on the entrance distance NOT EXCEEDING 24 nautical miles; 30 nm exceeds 24 nm, so the condition fails and the closing line between the natural entrance points cannot be drawn under that rule.
(2) 24 nautical miles, measured between the low-water marks of the natural entrance points.

3. GOVERNING TEXT
The controlling provision is Article 10 of UNCLOS. The operative paragraphs, as they appear verbatim in the sourced text (identical across the UN Part II page, the DOALOS compendium, the UN Audiovisual Library treaty text, and the UK reproduction at SI 2014/1353 Sch. 1):

  Article 10(2): 'For the purposes of this Convention, a bay is a well-marked indentation whose penetration is in such proportion to the width of its mouth as to contain land-locked waters and constitute more than a mere curvature of the coast. An indentation shall not, however, be regarded as a bay unless its area is as large as, or larger than, that of the semi-circle whose diameter is a line drawn across the mouth of that indentation.'

  Article 10(3): 'For the purpose of measurement, the area of an indentation is that lying between the low-water mark around the shore of the indentation and a line joining the low-water mark of its natural entrance points. Where, because of the presence of islands, an indentation has more than one mouth, the semi-circle shall be drawn on a line as long as the sum total of the lengths of the lines across the different mouths. Islands within an indentation shall be included as if they were part of the water area of the indentation.'

  Article 10(4): 'If the distance between the low-water marks of the natural entrance points of a bay does not exceed 24 nautical miles, a closing line may be drawn between these two low-water marks, and the waters enclosed thereby shall be considered as internal waters.'

  Article 10(5): 'Where the distance between the low-water marks of the natural entrance points of a bay exceeds 24 nautical miles, a straight baseline of 24 nautical miles shall be drawn within the bay in such a manner as to enclose the maximum area of water that is possible with a line of that length.'

  Article 10(6) (as reproduced in the UN Audiovisual Library text and the UNFSA/unclos_e.pdf text): 'The foregoing provisions do not apply to so-called "historic" bays, ...'

4. ANALYSIS
4.1 The rule is stated as a conditional. Article 10(4) is framed as 'If the distance ... does not exceed 24 nautical miles, a closing line may be drawn.' The permission ('may be drawn') is not free-standing; it exists only inside the stated condition. Outside the condition the permission does not exist. This is the ordinary reading of a conditional grant, and the passage itself supplies the alternative rule for the outside case in paragraph 5.

4.2 The measurement basis is the same one the reviewer used. Article 10(4) measures 'the distance between the low-water marks of the natural entrance points.' The reviewer's 30 nm figure is, on the stated assumption, measured the same way. There is therefore no measurement discrepancy to argue about: the figure is 30 nm on the convention's own basis, and 30 > 24.

4.3 The consequence of the 30 nm figure. Because the entrance exceeds 24 nm, Article 10(4) is inapplicable and Article 10(5) governs: 'a straight baseline of 24 nautical miles shall be drawn within the bay in such a manner as to enclose the maximum area of water that is possible with a line of that length.' The practical result is the opposite of what the reviewer asserts: (a) the closing line is drawn INSIDE the bay, not between the natural entrance points; (b) it is capped at 24 nm; (c) the waters enclosed by that inner line are internal waters, but the waters between that line and the natural entrance points are not enclosed as internal waters — they remain territorial sea (subject to the ordinary regime, including innocent passage), because the baseline there is the low-water line and the belt seaward of it is territorial sea under Articles 3 and 4.

4.4 Why the reviewer's proposition fails. It asserts an unconditional entitlement ('a bay with natural entrance points 30 nautical miles apart may have a closing line drawn between those low-water marks, making the enclosed waters internal waters') that the passage does not contain. The passage contains that entitlement only up to 24 nm. The reviewer has taken the correct rule and applied it past its stated ceiling.

4.5 Likely source of the error — flagged, not relied on. 24 nm is a number that appears in the law of the sea in more than one place (for example, the outer limit of the contiguous zone is 24 nm from the baselines, and the territorial sea breadth is up to 12 nm under Article 3). It is possible the reviewer has carried a 24 nm figure across from a different rule, or has assumed the bay closing line follows the outer territorial-sea geometry rather than the special bay rule. Nothing in the passage supports extending the bay closing line beyond 24 nm. On the facts given, the error is simply that 30 exceeds 24.

4.6 Conditions that sit alongside Article 10(4) — noted, and assumed not to change the outcome. Even for a bay whose entrance does NOT exceed 24 nm, the closing line is available only if: (a) the coasts of the bay belong to a single State (Art. 10(1)); (b) the indentation satisfies the definition and the semicircle-area test in Art. 10(2)–(3); and (c) the bay is not a 'historic' bay, to which the foregoing provisions do not apply (Art. 10(6)). These conditions are cumulative with the 24 nm ceiling and can only further restrict, never expand, the availability of the rule. Because the 30 nm entrance already defeats Article 10(4) on its own, the request's assumption that these other conditions do not alter the outcome is safe: the answer would be 'No' regardless of how they were resolved.

4.7 Scope note. This opinion addresses only the availability of the Article 10 closing-line rule. It does not address whether the waters in question could be enclosed as internal waters on some other basis (for example a historic title under Art. 10(6), straight baselines under Art. 7 where the geography is genuinely exceptional, or a river mouth under Art. 9). Those are separate routes requiring separate facts; none of them is the rule the reviewer stated, and none is established by the facts given.

5. CONCLUSIONS
(1) Is the rule available under the passage for a bay with natural entrance points 30 nm apart? No. Article 10(4)'s closing-line rule is conditional on the entrance distance not exceeding 24 nm; at 30 nm the condition is not met, and Article 10(5) instead requires a 24 nm straight baseline drawn within the bay enclosing the maximum area.
(2) Maximum entrance-point distance for the rule: 24 nautical miles, measured between the low-water marks of the natural entrance points (Art. 10(4)).

quotes.whole:
Space Law
Treaties & Principles
Convention on International Liability for Damage Caused by Space Objects
The Liability Convention was considered and negotiated by the Legal subcommittee from 1963 to 1972. Agreement was reached in the General Assembly in 1971 (
resolution 2777 (XXVI)), and the Convention entered into force in September 1972. Elaborating on
Article 7 of the Outer Space Treaty, the Liability Convention provides that a launching State shall be absolutely liable to pay compensation for damage caused by its space objects on the surface of the Earth or to aircraft, and liable for damage due to its faults in space. The Convention also provides for procedures for the settlement of claims for damages.

verdict.summary:
Scope and source

This answers the question against Article II of the 1972 Convention on International Liability for Damage Caused by Space Objects, the provision that establishes absolute liability for damage caused by a space object on the surface of the earth or to aircraft in flight. The quoted text was retrieved from the public UNOOSA and FAA versions of the Convention.

Ask 1 — Does the passage stating absolute liability give a monetary cap?

No. Article II contains no monetary cap. It states no ceiling, no fixed sum, no formula, no maximum amount, and no cross-reference to a monetary limit. The provision is a single sentence establishing liability and the obligation to pay compensation; it does not quantify compensation.

Ask 2 — What the passage does say about liability

Article II states:

"A launching State shall be absolutely liable to pay compensation for damage caused by its space object on the surface of the earth or to aircraft in flight."

(One UNOOSA rendering reads "to aircraft flight"; the FAA and Lovdata texts read "to aircraft in flight." The difference is a textual/typographical variance and does not affect the answer.)

The passage therefore says, in substance:

1. The liable party is a "launching State."
2. The standard of liability is "absolutely liable" — i.e., liability is not conditioned on fault in the text of Article II.
3. The obligation is "to pay compensation."
4. The damage must be "caused by its space object."
5. The damage must occur "on the surface of the earth or to aircraft in flight."

What the passage does not say

Article II does not state a monetary cap; it does not state any monetary amount; it does not prescribe a formula for calculating compensation; it does not set a maximum recoverable sum; and it does not refer to another provision that sets a cap. Absolute liability under Article II is a standard of liability, not a limitation on the amount of compensation.

This answer is confined to the absolute-liability passage. It does not opine on whether any other provision of the Convention, outside Article II, addresses the measure or limits of compensation; that would require a separate review of the full text. For the auditor's question as framed, the operative answer is: no monetary cap appears in Article II, and Article II says only that the launching State is absolutely liable to pay compensation for damage caused by its space object on the surface of the earth or to aircraft in flight.

Commentary
(1) Article 53 covers the termination of treaties which
neither contain any provision regarding their duration
or termination nor mention any right for the parties
to denounce or withdraw from them. Such treaties are
not uncommon, recent examples being the four Geneva
Conventions on the Law of the Sea and the Vienna
Convention on Diplomatic Relations. The question is
whether they are to be regarded as terminable only by
unanimous agreement or whether individual parties are
under any conditions to be considered as having an
implied right to withdraw from the treaty upon giving
reasonable notice to that effect.

is established that the parties intended to admit the possibility of denunciation or
withdrawal or if a right of denunciation or withdrawal may be implied by the

verdict.summary:
IDENTIFICATION OF THE INSTRUMENT AND PROVISION

The supplied UN treaty text is the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties (Vienna, 23 May 1969), Part V, Section 3 ('Termination and Suspension of the Operation of Treaties'), Article 56, headed 'Denunciation of or withdrawal from a treaty containing no provision regarding termination, denunciation or withdrawal'. The operative text, as it appears in the supplied document, reads:

  'Article 56
   Denunciation of or withdrawal from a treaty containing no
   provision regarding termination, denunciation or withdrawal
   1. A treaty which contains no provision regarding its termination and which does not provide for denunciation or withdrawal is not subject to denunciation or withdrawal unless:
   (a) it is established that the parties intended to admit the possibility of denunciation or withdrawal; or
   (b) a right of denunciation or withdrawal may be implied by the nature of the treaty.
   2. A party shall give not less than twelve months' notice of its intention to denounce or withdraw from a treaty under paragraph 1.'

ANSWER

Minimum notice period: twelve (12) months. Unit: months.

Ground: Article 56, paragraph 2, second sentence — 'not less than twelve months' notice'. Because the text says 'not less than', twelve months is a floor: a notice shorter than twelve months does not satisfy Article 56(2); a longer notice does.

WHY 'PARAGRAPH 1' POINTS HERE

1. The request's phrase 'under paragraph 1' is not a free-floating description: it is the exact cross-reference written into Article 56(2) ('... from a treaty under paragraph 1'). No other denunciation/withdrawal provision in the Convention carries that formulation.
2. Paragraph 1 itself contains no period. It supplies only the conditions under which a treaty that is silent on termination, denunciation and withdrawal may nonetheless be denounced (intention of the parties, or implication from the nature of the treaty). The notice requirement is deliberately placed in paragraph 2, which is why a reader who stops at paragraph 1 will find no figure and must read on to paragraph 2.
3. Corroboration inside the supplied corpus:
   - ILC Commentary to draft article 53 (1966), paragraph (6): '... it preferred in paragraph 2 to specify that not less than twelve months' notice must be given of an intention to denounce or withdraw from a treaty under the present article.'
   - Draft article 53(2), 1966: 'A party shall give not less than twelve months' notice of its intention to denounce or withdraw from a treaty under paragraph 1 of this article.'
   - 1979 redraft (A/CN.4/L.300), Article 56(2): 'A party shall give not less than twelve months notice of its intention to denounce or withdraw from a treaty under paragraph 1.'
   - UN publication on the fulfilment of Charter obligations: 'A party must give at least 12 months' notice of its intention to denounce or withdraw from a treaty (see article 56 of the Vienna Convention, 1969).'
All four independent renderings in the supplied material give the same figure: twelve months.

HOW TO APPLY IT (operational rule)

- Start the clock at the date the notice of intention to denounce or withdraw is given (received by the counterparty/depositary as the treaty or the applicable procedural articles require).
- The earliest date on which the denunciation or withdrawal may take effect is that date plus twelve months. Notice given on day D supports an effective date no earlier than D + 12 months.
- Do not confuse the notice period with the eligibility gate. Article 56 does not require any period of membership before notice may be given; the three-year and four-year gates that appear elsewhere in the supplied material (e.g. the chemical-weapons-type and ozone-layer-type clauses quoted in the UN publication) belong to other conventions and do not modify Article 56.
- The figure is a default, not a mandatory term of every treaty: Article 56 applies only where the treaty is silent. Where the treaty itself fixes a period (six months, one year, ninety days, etc. — all of which appear in the supplied material for other instruments), that treaty provision prevails, and Article 56(2)'s twelve months is displaced.

CAVEATS DISCLOSED RATHER THAN HIDDEN

- The file does not name the convention. The identification above rests on the fact that the supplied text is the Vienna Convention text and that the 'paragraph 1' cross-reference is unique to Article 56(2) within it. If the underlying file were in truth a different instrument (e.g. one of the conventions quoted in the same corpus providing six months or one year), the answer would change; on the text supplied, it is twelve months.
- The question asks for the minimum, which the text itself fixes as a floor ('not less than'); it is not a maximum and no upper bound is imposed by Article 56(2).
- Article 56(2) governs denunciation and withdrawal indifferently; the text uses the two verbs in the same sentence, so no separate figure applies to one but not the other.

CONCLUSION

Under paragraph 1 of the relevant article — Article 56 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, 1969 — the minimum notice a party must give of its intention to denounce or withdraw is twelve months.

in months

verdict.summary:
The relevant instrument is the Optional Protocol to the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations concerning the Compulsory Settlement of Disputes (Vienna, 24 April 1963).

Article III(1) provides: "Within the same period of two months, the parties may agree to adopt a conciliation procedure before resorting to the International Court of Justice." The "same period of two months" is the period stated in Article II, i.e. two months after one party has notified its opinion to the other that a dispute exists.

Article III(2) provides: "The conciliation commission shall, unless the parties otherwise agree, make its recommendations within five months after its appointment."

The requested calculation is arithmetic only:

2 months (period for agreeing to adopt a conciliation procedure) + 5 months (period after the commission's appointment for it to make recommendations) = 7 months.

The two periods are distinct: the first is a window for the parties to agree to a conciliation procedure; the second is the default period for the conciliation commission's recommendations after its appointment. The resulting 7 months is not a composite or continuous deadline measured from notification of the dispute, and it should not be treated as one. The qualification "unless the parties otherwise agree" in Article III(2) does not alter the stated five-month figure for purposes of this sum.

24 April 2017

Overview
The fourth edition of the World Health Organization’s (WHO) Guidelines for drinking-water quality (GDWQ) builds on over 50 years of guidance by WHO on drinking-water quality, which has formed an authoritative basis for the setting of national regulations
and standards for water safety in support of public health.
It is the product of significant revisions to clarify and elaborate on ways of implementing its recommendations of contextual hazard identification and risk management, through the establishment of health-based targets, catchment-to-consumer water safety
plans and independent surveillance.
This first addendum updates the fourth edition. Updates reflect new evidence and further, provides additional explanations to support better understanding and application of the guidance.

Overview
This first addendum to the fourth edition of the Guidelines for drinking-water quality (GDWQ) details the changes that have been made to the fourth edition of the GDWQ. Updates reflect new evidence and further, provides additional explanations to support better understanding and application of the guidance.
The key updates in the first addendum include updated or revised risk assessments and/or guideline values or health-based values for barium; bentazone; chlorine dioxide, chlorate and chlorite; dichlorvos; dicofol; diquat; lead; MCPA; nitrate and nitrite; and perchlorate. Additional guidance on risk management considerations and monitoring of lead is provided, alongside new guidance on microbial risk assessment, aggregating multiple barriers for overall water treatment performance and microbial detection methods.

Abstract

Access to safe drinking-water is essential to health, a basic human right and a key component of public health protection. This first addendum to the fourth edition of the Guidelines for drinking-water quality updates the existing guidance to reflect new scientific evidence and provide additional clarification to support its implementation. The document forms part of WHO’s rolling revision process and is intended primarily for water and health regulators, policy-makers and their advisers in developing national drinking-water policies, regulations and risk management approaches.

The addendum introduces new and revised risk assessments, guideline values and health-based values for selected chemical contaminants, including pesticides and other priority substances, together with updated guidance on lead risk management, microbial risk assessment, water treatment performance and microbial detection methods. It also expands supporting information on water safety plans, source water protection, surveillance, emergency situations and the application of preventive, risk-based approaches from catchment to consumer. In addition, the publication incorporates references to new supporting documents and clarifies concepts and terminology to improve consistency and facilitate the practical application of the Guidelines across a wide range of settings.

Abstract

Access to safe drinking-water is fundamental to public health, human well-being and sustainable development. This publication presents the fourth edition of the WHO Guidelines for drinking-water quality, incorporating the first addendum, and provides a comprehensive framework for managing risks that may compromise the safety of drinking-water. The Guidelines are intended primarily for regulators, policy-makers and their advisers, supporting the development of national policies, standards and regulations based on preventive risk management from catchment to consumer. They address microbial, chemical, radiological and acceptability aspects of drinking-water quality, together with the roles of surveillance, health-based targets and water safety plans.

The publication further develops concepts introduced in previous editions, including the multiple-barrier approach to drinking-water safety, the application of water safety plans, quantitative risk assessment and guidance for a wide range of supply systems and specific circumstances. It includes updated scientific information, revised and new guideline values and health-based values for selected contaminants, expanded guidance on microbial hazards, climate change, emergency situations and pesticides used for vector control, as well as detailed fact sheets, supporting documentation and practical guidance to facilitate implementation in diverse national and local contexts.

verdict.summary:
COMPLIANCE NOTE — WHO GDWQ CITATION CORRECTION (source-of-record reading)

1. SOURCE OF RECORD (satisfies the constraint in ask 1)
Page read: https://www.who.int/publications-detail-redirect/9789241549950 — titled 'Guidelines for drinking-water quality, 4th edition, incorporating the 1st addendum', dated 24 April 2017, ISBN 978-92-4-154995-0, 631 pages. Retrieved 2026-11-23T12:11:42Z, page sha256 fd30af1de1bd. All quotations below marked [P] are taken verbatim from this page. Nothing in this note is drawn from outside the supplied page text except where explicitly labelled [CORROBORATION].

2. ASK 2 — WHAT UPDATED VERSION THE PAGE TELLS READERS TO ACCESS
[P] verbatim, closing line of the Overview section:

  'Access here the latest and updated version of this publication: Guidelines for drinking-water quality - Fourth edition incorporating the first and second addenda'

Answer (identifier to be used in the compliance file): Guidelines for drinking-water quality - Fourth edition incorporating the first and second addenda.

Reading notes for the compliance file:
- The page does not name a fifth edition. The 'updated version' it points to is still the fourth edition — but the fourth edition as amended by BOTH the first and the second addenda. Any file wording that stops at 'fourth edition', or at 'fourth edition incorporating the first addendum', is therefore stale by one addendum.
- The page gives no ISBN, publication date or URL for the newer version; it gives only the title string above. Do not manufacture an ISBN or date for it in the compliance file. If an ISBN/URL is required by the citation style, that element must be sourced from the newer version's own page and is outside this page's text.
- The page's own title uses the hyphenless form '4th edition, incorporating the 1st addendum'; the directive sentence uses 'Fourth edition incorporating the first and second addenda'. Reproduce the directive sentence's wording as the current-version identifier, since that is the sentence that designates currency.

3. ASK 3 — WHAT THE PAGE SAYS THE FIRST ADDENDUM DOES
[P] verbatim, Overview section:

  'This first addendum updates the fourth edition. Updates reflect new evidence and further, provides additional explanations to support better understanding and application of the guidance.'

('and further, provides' is reproduced exactly as published; it is a drafting slip in the WHO text and should be quoted with [sic] if the compliance file requires strict verbatim reproduction.)

[P] verbatim, 'More information' block on the same page:

  'View the detailed list of changes in the first addendum to the fourth edition of the GDWQ'

So, on the supplied page's own words, the first addendum does two things: (i) it updates the fourth edition, with updates reflecting new evidence; and (ii) it provides additional explanations to support better understanding and application of the guidance.

[CORROBORATION — not the supplied page] The standalone 1st-addendum page (https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241550017, 20 February 2017, ISBN 978-92-4-155001-7, 137 pp.) describes the same addendum more specifically: it 'details the changes that have been made to the fourth edition'; key updates cover revised risk assessments and/or guideline values or health-based values for barium, bentazone, chlorine dioxide/chlorate/chlorite, dichlorvos, dicofol, diquat, lead, MCPA, nitrate and nitrite, and perchlorate; plus additional risk-management and monitoring guidance on lead, and new guidance on microbial risk assessment, aggregating multiple barriers for overall water treatment performance, and microbial detection methods. Use this detail only if the compliance file wants the substance of the addendum; it is not what the supplied page says, and must be attributed to the addendum page, not to 9789241549950.

4. CORRECTED CITATION FOR THE COMPLIANCE FILE
Replace the existing 'fourth edition' entry with:

  WHO. Guidelines for drinking-water quality — Fourth edition incorporating the first and second addenda. Geneva: World Health Organization. [Current version as designated on WHO publication page 9789241549950, retrieved 2026-11-23.] Supersedes: WHO (2017) Guidelines for drinking-water quality, 4th edition incorporating the 1st addendum, ISBN 978-92-4-154995-0, https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/254637.

Where the compliance file also cites the first addendum in its own right, keep:

  WHO (2017). Guidelines for drinking-water quality: first addendum to the fourth edition, 1st add., 4th ed. ISBN 978-92-4-155001-7. https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/254636.

And describe the addendum's function in the file as: 'updates the fourth edition, with updates reflecting new evidence, and provides additional explanations to support better understanding and application of the guidance.'

5. RETENTION / AUDIT TRAIL
The IRIS record for the first-addendum-incorporating edition (https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/254637) carries the note [CORROBORATION]: 'Updated version with second addendum available here: https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/352532'. This independently corroborates ask 2's direction of travel, but the compliance file's stated basis for the change should be the WHO publication page sentence quoted in §2, with the retrieval date recorded, since a live web page can change after capture.

6. WHAT THIS NOTE DOES NOT ESTABLISH
- It does not state a publication date, ISBN or handle for the first-and-second-addenda version (not given on the supplied page).
- It does not claim a fifth edition exists or is referenced.
- It does not verify that the page is current as of the file's review date; the retrieval timestamp above is the only currency evidence available and should be recorded alongside the citation.
- It does not substitute for checking the rest of the compliance file for other instances of the bare 'fourth edition' string; the correction above should be applied to every occurrence, including any that appear in narrative text rather than in the reference list.

verdict.summary:
RFC 7519 — RULE FOR DUPLICATE CLAIM NAMES IN A JWT CLAIMS SET

1. VERBATIM NORMATIVE TEXT

Source: RFC 7519 (JSON Web Token (JWT)), May 2015, Section 4 ("JWT Claims"), first paragraph. The paragraph appears immediately after the sentence defining the Claims Set as a JSON object and immediately before "The set of claims that a JWT must contain to be considered valid is context dependent...".

The text, exactly as it appears in the RFC:

    The JWT Claims Set represents a JSON object whose members are the
    claims conveyed by the JWT.  The Claim Names within a JWT Claims Set
    MUST be unique; JWT parsers MUST either reject JWTs with duplicate
    Claim Names or use a JSON parser that returns only the lexically last
    duplicate member name, as specified in Section 15.12 ("The JSON
    Object") of ECMAScript 5.1 [ECMAScript].

That is the answer. Everything below is decomposition, scope, and engineering consequence.

2. NORMATIVE DECOMPOSITION

The paragraph contains three distinct obligations, on three distinct actors:

  O1. Producers / the data model — "The Claim Names within a JWT Claims Set MUST be unique." This is a requirement on the Claims Set itself: a conforming JWT Claims Set never contains the same Claim Name twice. A token with duplicate Claim Names is a non-conforming Claims Set.

  O2. Parsers, option A — "JWT parsers MUST either reject JWTs with duplicate Claim Names ...". A parser satisfies the rule by detecting duplication and refusing the token.

  O3. Parsers, option B — "... or use a JSON parser that returns only the lexically last duplicate member name, as specified in Section 15.12 ("The JSON Object") of ECMAScript 5.1 [ECMAScript]." A parser satisfies the rule by collapsing duplicates deterministically to the last occurrence in document order.

O2 and O3 are alternatives joined by "either ... or"; the RFC mandates that a parser do one of them. It does not mandate which. A parser that keeps the FIRST occurrence, that keeps a nondeterministic occurrence, that merges values, or that silently accepts duplicates and leaves the resolution to whichever JSON library is linked, violates the MUST.

3. SCOPE OF THE RULE

  - It lives in Section 4, not Section 4.1. It therefore applies to all Claim Names, not just the Registered Claim Names (iss, sub, aud, exp, nbf, iat, jti). It applies equally to Public Claim Names (Section 4.2) and Private Claim Names (Section 4.3). A duplicate private claim name is as much a violation as a duplicate "iss".
  - It applies to the JWT Claims Set regardless of how the JWT is represented. Per Section 3, the Claims Set is the JWS Payload when the JWT is a JWS, and the JWE plaintext when the JWT is a JWE. The rule attaches to the Claims Set, so it binds in both representations and in nested JWS/JWE constructions.
  - It is about member names of the Claims Set object (the top-level members). A JSON object nested inside a claim value that happens to contain duplicate names is not a duplicate "Claim Name" under this paragraph; the RFC's sentence is scoped to "the Claim Names within a JWT Claims Set".
  - Duplicate means the same member name string. JSON member names are compared as strings; "iss" and "ISS" are different names, and neither is a duplicate of the other.
  - Out of scope of this paragraph: the JOSE Header. The quoted rule speaks only of the JWT Claims Set. Do not cite RFC 7519 Section 4 as authority for duplicate-parameter handling in the protected/unprotected header; that is a different question with a different source.

4. WHAT THE RFC DOES NOT SAY (frequently mis-cited)

  - It does not require rejection. Rejection is one of two permitted behaviours.
  - It does not specify an error code, error type, or HTTP status for rejection. "Reject" is left unqualified; the application layer chooses the failure surface.
  - It does not say the whole JWT is invalid versus just the duplicated claim. Under O2 the token is rejected; under O3 the token is accepted with the last value. There is no third "drop the claim and continue" option in the text.
  - It does not define "lexically last" as alphabetically greatest. In ECMAScript 5.1 Section 15.12 the operative notion is the last occurrence in the text of the object. "Lexically last" here means last in lexical (document) order. Implementations that sort names or compare strings to pick a winner are not implementing option B.
  - It does not say the two options are equally safe. See Section 6.

5. IMPLEMENTATION PROCEDURE

Recommended default for new code: option A (strict rejection). It is the only option that is identical across every component in a pipeline, so it cannot be exploited by a parser-differential attack.

5.1 Strict parser (option A), Python 3, enforcing the rule at the Claims Set level only:

    import json

    class DuplicateClaimName(ValueError):
        """RFC 7519 Section 4: Claim Names within a JWT Claims Set MUST be unique."""
        def __init__(self, name):
            super().__init__(f"duplicate Claim Name in JWT Claims Set: {name!r}")
            self.name = name

    class _Members(list):
        """Marker so we can tell a JSON object from a JSON array."""
        pass

    def _collect(pairs):
        return _Members(pairs)   # preserves order AND duplicates

    def parse_claims_strict(payload: bytes) -> dict:
        top = json.loads(payload.decode("utf-8"), object_pairs_hook=_collect)
        if not isinstance(top, _Members):
            raise ValueError("JWT Claims Set must be a JSON object")
        claims = {}
        for name, value in top:
            if name in claims:
                raise DuplicateClaimName(name)   # O2: reject
            claims[name] = value
        return _normalize(claims)

    def _normalize(node):
        # Nested objects were also captured as _Members; convert them to dicts
        # (last-wins inside nested values is NOT governed by RFC 7519 Section 4).
        if isinstance(node, _Members):
            out = {}
            for k, v in node:
                out[k] = _normalize(v)
            return out
        if isinstance(node, list):
            return [_normalize(v) for v in node]
        return node

    Note on why object_pairs_hook is required: a plain json.loads silently applies last-wins to every object and destroys the evidence that a duplicate existed. Duplicate detection is impossible after a normal parse. The same is true of most default JSON bindings in other languages (JavaScript JSON.parse, Go encoding/json into map, Java Jackson into Map, .NET System.Text.Json into Dictionary) — each silently keeps one value, and not always the same one.

5.2 Option B parser (last-in-document-order wins), for interop with peers that demand it:

    def parse_claims_last_wins(payload: bytes) -> dict:
        top = json.loads(payload.decode("utf-8"), object_pairs_hook=_collect)
        if not isinstance(top, _Members):
            raise ValueError("JWT Claims Set must be a JSON object")
        claims = {}
        for name, value in top:
            claims[name] = value      # later occurrence overwrites earlier one
        return _normalize(claims)

    Correctness note: this satisfies O3 because Python dict assignment in iteration order keeps the final occurrence in document order. It would NOT satisfy O3 if the pairs were sorted first, or if "last" were taken to mean max(name).

5.3 Placement in the validation pipeline. Run the duplicate check on the decoded Claims Set bytes BEFORE any claim is consumed for authorization decisions, and before signature verification is relied upon for trust. Ordering matters: signature verification proves the bytes were signed, not that the Claims Set was well-formed. A token with a valid signature over a Claims Set containing two "sub" members is a validly-signed non-conforming JWT, and must still be rejected under option A.

6. SECURITY RATIONALE FOR PREFERRING OPTION A

Option B is legal but is the classic parser-differential hazard: if the JWT passes through two components that both implement option B differently — or one that implements option A and one that implements B — the value that the authorization layer sees may not be the value that the issuer intended or that the audit log records. A token carrying two "sub" or two "aud" members can be made to authenticate as one principal at the gateway and be logged as another. Because RFC 7519 permits rejection outright, rejecting costs nothing in conformance and eliminates the class. Deployments that must accept option B should confine duplicate resolution to a single trusted library and never re-serialize/re-parse the Claims Set downstream.

7. TEST VECTORS

Each payload below is the raw JSON to be base64url-encoded into the JWS/JWE payload segment (encoding omitted deliberately; the JSON is the test input).

  T1  {"iss":"https://as.example","sub":"alice","aud":"api"}
      No duplicates. Option A: accept. Option B: accept.

  T2  {"iss":"https://as.example","sub":"alice","sub":"admin"}
      Duplicate "sub". Option A: reject with DuplicateClaimName('sub'). Option B: accept with sub == "admin".

  T3  {"iss":"https://as.example","sub":"admin","sub":"alice"}
      Duplicate "sub", reversed order. Option A: reject. Option B: accept with sub == "alice". T2 and T3 together prove the implementation is order-sensitive, as option B requires.

  T4  {"aud":"api","exp":1700000000,"aud":"api"}
      Duplicate with identical values. Still a duplicate Claim Name; the rule is about names, not values. Option A: reject. Option B: accept.

  T5  {"iss":"a","ISS":"b"}
      Not a duplicate — names differ in case. Option A: accept. Option B: accept.

  T6  {"sub":"alice","meta":{"k":1,"k":2}}
      Duplicate inside a nested value, not at the Claims Set level. Option A: accept the Claims Set (nested resolution is application policy, outside RFC 7519 Section 4). Option B: accept.

  T7  {"sub":"alice","sub":"admin","iss":"https://as.example","sub":"root"}
      Triple duplicate. Option A: reject. Option B: accept with sub == "root" (last in document order, not max string).

  T8  A Claims Set that is a JSON array or scalar, e.g. ["alice"]
      Not an object, therefore not a valid Claims Set. Reject before duplicate analysis.

8. CONFORMANCE CHECKLIST

  [ ] Duplicate detection runs on the raw decoded Claims Set bytes, not on an already-parsed map.
  [ ] The chosen behaviour is exactly one of: reject, or last-in-document-order-wins. Never first-wins, never nondeterministic.
  [ ] Detection is applied to all Claim Name classes, not only Registered Claim Names.
  [ ] Detection is applied at the Claims Set top level; nested-object duplicate policy is documented separately.
  [ ] Claim Name comparison is exact string comparison, case-sensitive.
  [ ] The check executes before any claim value influences authorization or audit output.
  [ ] The rejection path produces a distinguishable, logged error (name of the offending claim) rather than a generic parse failure.
  [ ] The behaviour is identical in every component that parses the token in the request path.

9. ONE-SENTENCE RESTATEMENT FOR CITATION

RFC 7519 Section 4 requires Claim Names within a JWT Claims Set to be unique, and requires JWT parsers either to reject JWTs with duplicate Claim Names or to use a JSON parser that returns only the lexically last duplicate member name, per ECMAScript 5.1 Section 15.12.

signature algorithm as defined in Section 8.2 of RFC 3447 [RFC3447]

private key.  This is the JWS Signature value.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER

RFC 7519 (JWT), Section 8 ("Implementation Requirements"), states normatively that exactly two of the signature/MAC algorithm identifiers registered by JSON Web Algorithms (JWA = RFC 7518) MUST be implemented by a conforming JWT implementation:

  1. HS256 — HMAC using SHA-256 (a MAC algorithm, RFC 7518 §3.2)
  2. none  — the unsecured JWS mode, i.e. no signature/MAC at all (RFC 7515 §4.1.1 / Appendix A.5)

Everything else in the JWS signature/MAC family is at most RECOMMENDED or OPTIONAL.

VERBATIM SOURCE (RFC 7519 §8, fetched from rfc-editor.org):

  "Of the signature and MAC algorithms specified in JSON Web Algorithms
   [JWA], only HMAC SHA-256 (\"HS256\") and \"none\" MUST be implemented by
   conforming JWT implementations.  It is RECOMMENDED that
   implementations also support RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 with the SHA-256 hash
   algorithm (\"RS256\") and ECDSA using the P-256 curve and the SHA-256
   hash algorithm (\"ES256\").  Support for other algorithms and key sizes
   is OPTIONAL."

Corroborating registry entry (RFC 7518 §7.1.2, IANA "JSON Web Signature and Encryption Algorithms"): Algorithm Name "HS256", Description "HMAC using SHA-256", Usage Location(s) "alg", JOSE Implementation Requirements: **Required**. HS384 and HS512 are listed as **Optional** in the same registry.

REQUIREMENT LEVELS FOR THE FULL JWS SIGNATURE/MAC SET (per RFC 7519 §8)

  | alg    | Algorithm                                  | RFC 7519 §8 level |
  |--------|--------------------------------------------|-------------------|
  | HS256  | HMAC using SHA-256                         | MUST              |
  | none   | No digital signature or MAC                | MUST              |
  | RS256  | RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 using SHA-256             | RECOMMENDED       |
  | ES256  | ECDSA using P-256 curve and SHA-256        | RECOMMENDED       |
  | HS384  | HMAC using SHA-384                         | OPTIONAL          |
  | HS512  | HMAC using SHA-512                         | OPTIONAL          |
  | RS384  | RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 using SHA-384             | OPTIONAL          |
  | RS512  | RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 using SHA-512             | OPTIONAL          |
  | ES384  | ECDSA using P-384 curve and SHA-384        | OPTIONAL          |
  | ES512  | ECDSA using P-521 curve and SHA-512        | OPTIONAL          |
  | PS256  | RSASSA-PSS using SHA-256 and MGF1(SHA-256)  | OPTIONAL          |
  | PS384  | RSASSA-PSS using SHA-384 and MGF1(SHA-384)  | OPTIONAL          |
  | PS512  | RSASSA-PSS using SHA-512 and MGF1(SHA-512)  | OPTIONAL          |

("Support for other algorithms and key sizes is OPTIONAL" is the catch-all clause covering every row not marked MUST/RECOMMENDED.)

INTERPRETATION NOTES AN IMPLEMENTER MUST GET RIGHT

1. "MUST" is a two-element set, and one element is the absence of a signature. The only *cryptographic* algorithm a conforming JWT implementation is required to implement is HS256. "none" is the unsecured JWS variant; implementing it means being able to parse/produce a JWS with `"alg":"none"` and an empty signature segment. Consequently a conforming implementation is NOT required to implement any public-key digital signature algorithm — RS256 and ES256 are RECOMMENDED, not MUST.

2. "none" MUST be implemented ≠ "none" may be accepted. RFC 7519 §8 is an implementation-capability requirement. Acceptance is a separate policy decision: a JWT consumer must not treat `"alg":"none"` as valid unless the application has explicitly opted in to unsecured JWTs; otherwise it is an algorithm-confusion / signature-stripping vulnerability. Implementing "none" and then rejecting it at the verification boundary is compliant.

3. HS256 carries a key-size constraint from JWA (RFC 7518 §3.2): "A key of the same size as the hash output (e.g., 256 bits for 'HS256') or larger MUST be used with this algorithm." So an HS256 implementation that accepts a shared secret shorter than 256 bits is not conformant with JWA even though it implements the algorithm identifier. RFC 7518's rationale cites NIST SP 800-107 §5.3.4: effective security strength is the minimum of the key's strength and twice the internal hash size.

4. Scope. This answer is scoped to signature and MAC algorithms (`alg` values used with JWS/JWT). The same RFC 7519 §8 paragraph separately mandates, only if encryption is offered at all, RSA1_5, A128KW, A256KW, A128CBC-HS256 and A256CBC-HS512 — that is a JWE requirement and is not part of the answer to this ask.

5. Normative references. RFC 7519 does not itself define algorithms; it defers to JWA (RFC 7518) and JWS (RFC 7515). The MUST statement above lives in RFC 7519 §8; the algorithm definitions and the "Required" registry marking for HS256 live in RFC 7518 §3.2 and §7.1.2 respectively.

6. Currency caveat. The RFC Editor's info page for RFC 7518 carries the banner "This RFC was updated, see RFC 9864." I have not retrieved or verified the text of RFC 9864, so I do not characterize its contents here. The answer above states RFC 7519 §8 / RFC 7518 as published (May 2015). Before relying on this for a security review, check RFC 9864 (and the RFC 7519 errata) for any change affecting the standing of "none" — the likely area of impact — while noting that HS256's status is not in question in any source I have seen.

SHORT FORM FOR A SPEC/TEST-MATRIX LINE

  Required by RFC 7519 §8 for conforming JWT implementations:
    HS256 (HMAC-SHA-256) — MUST
    none (unsecured JWS) — MUST
  Recommended: RS256, ES256
  All others (HS384, HS512, RS384, RS512, ES384, ES512, PS256, PS384, PS512, and any non-registered alg): OPTIONAL

1. "MUST" is a two-element set, and one element is the absence of a signature. The only *cryptographic* algorithm a conforming JWT implementation is required to implement is HS256. "none" is the unsecured JWS variant; implementing it means being able to parse/produce a JWS with `"alg":"none"` and an empty signature segment. Consequently a conforming implementation is NOT required to implement any public-key digital signature algorithm — RS256 and ES256 are RECOMMENDED, not MUST.

2. "none" MUST be implemented ≠ "none" may be accepted. RFC 7519 §8 is an implementation-capability requirement. Acceptance is a separate policy decision: a JWT consumer must not treat `"alg":"none"` as valid unless the application has explicitly opted in to unsecured JWTs; otherwise it is an algorithm-confusion / signature-stripping vulnerability. Implementing "none" and then rejecting it at the verification boundary is compliant.

3. HS256 carries a key-size constraint from JWA (RFC 7518 §3.2): "A key of the same size as the hash output (e.g., 256 bits for 'HS256') or larger MUST be used with this algorithm." So an HS256 implementation that accepts a shared secret shorter than 256 bits is not conformant with JWA even though it implements the algorithm identifier. RFC 7518's rationale cites NIST SP 800-107 §5.3.4: effective security strength is the minimum of the key's strength and twice the internal hash size.

4. Scope. This answer is scoped to signature and MAC algorithms (`alg` values used with JWS/JWT). The same RFC 7519 §8 paragraph separately mandates, only if encryption is offered at all, RSA1_5, A128KW, A256KW, A128CBC-HS256 and A256CBC-HS512 — that is a JWE requirement and is not part of the answer to this ask.

5. Normative references. RFC 7519 does not itself define algorithms; it defers to JWA (RFC 7518) and JWS (RFC 7515). The MUST statement above lives in RFC 7519 §8; the algorithm definitions and the "Required" registry marking for HS256 live in RFC 7518 §3.2 and §7.1.2 respectively.

6. Currency caveat. The RFC Editor's info page for RFC 7518 carries the banner "This RFC was updated, see RFC 9864." I have not retrieved or verified the text of RFC 9864, so I do not characterize its contents here. The answer above states RFC 7519 §8 / RFC 7518 as published (May 2015). Before relying on this for a security review, check RFC 9864 (and the RFC 7519 errata) for any change affecting the standing of "none" — the likely area of impact — while noting that HS256's status is not in question in any source I have seen.

SHORT FORM FOR A SPEC/TEST-MATRIX LINE

  Required by RFC 7519 §8 for conforming JWT implementations:
    HS256 (HMAC-SHA-256) — MUST
    none (unsecured JWS) — MUST
  Recommended: RS256, ES256
  All others (HS384, HS512, RS384, RS512, ES384, ES512, PS256, PS384, PS512, and any non-registered alg): OPTIONAL

7.2.  JWS JSON Serialization
The JWS JSON Serialization represents digitally signed or MACed
content as a JSON object.  This representation is neither optimized
for compactness nor URL-safe.
Two closely related syntaxes are defined for the JWS JSON
Serialization: a fully general syntax, with which content can be
secured with more than one digital signature and/or MAC operation,
and a flattened syntax, which is optimized for the single digital
signature or MAC case.

Parameter values are not integrity protected.
signature
The "signature" member MUST be present and contain the value
BASE64URL(JWS Signature).

7.2.2 Flattened JWS JSON Serialization Syntax​
The flattened JWS JSON Serialization syntax is based upon the general syntax but flattens it, optimizing it for the single digital signature/MAC case. It flattens it by removing the "signatures" member and instead placing those members defined for use in the "signatures" array (the "protected", "header", and "signature" members) in the top-level JSON object (at the same level as the "payload" member).
The "signatures" member MUST NOT be present when using this syntax. Other than this syntax difference, JWS JSON Serialization objects using the flattened syntax are processed identically to those using the general syntax.

{
"payload":"<payload contents>",
"protected":"<integrity-protected header contents>",
"header":<non-integrity-protected header contents>,

}

JWT allows the signature or MAC to contain public key, certificates or urls
pointing to certificates. This is a design mistake because in verification,
signature and MAC are under attacker control which lead to various attacks.
Therefore, in our API, once the key is configured by users, it can not be

system and jeopardizes its security.

one side generates the signature and the other side verifies the signature.

quotes.whole:
There is no way to tell whether the key should be used as encryption key or HMAC
key. Even if we know that it’s used as HMAC key, we still don’t know what hash
function should be used during HMAC verification. One way to mitigate this issue
is to enforce the field “alg” as defined at
https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7517#section-4. Key without “alg” field is
rejected. Note that for signer, we only support 1 key. There are 2 reasons:
Signer with multiple keys is rare, even in key rotation. The typical use
case is that the signer switches to new key immediately, while the verifier
has some grace period to use both the old key and a new key for
verification. Furthermore, if the user needs to use multiple keys in
signing, it’s trivial to just create 2 signers; it’s inconvenient but it
doesn’t harm security.
To support multiple keys, we have to specify the primary key and default
key, otherwise the signer wouldn’t know which key should be used to sign
data. This makes the design and implementation unnecessary complicated for
the main use case.
Installation
To install jws:
git clone https://github.com/google/jws
cd jws
sudo python setup.py install
To test jws: sudo python setup.py test

verdict.summary:
RFC 7515 (JSON Web Signature, JWS), Section 7.1 'JWS Compact Serialization', states normatively:

  'Only one signature/MAC is supported by the JWS Compact Serialization and it provides no syntax to represent a JWS Unprotected Header value.'

Answers

1. Number of signatures or MACs supported by the JWS Compact Serialization: 1 (exactly one signature or MAC value).

2. Header syntax it lacks: the JWS Unprotected Header — i.e., there is no syntax in the Compact Serialization to represent an unprotected header. The Compact Serialization carries only the JWS Protected Header, so the JOSE Header is identical to the JWS Protected Header.

Supporting normative text

- Section 3.1 (JWS Compact Serialization Overview): 'In the JWS Compact Serialization, no JWS Unprotected Header is used. In this case, the JOSE Header and the JWS Protected Header are the same.' The serialization is exactly:

    BASE64URL(UTF8(JWS Protected Header)) || '.' ||
    BASE64URL(JWS Payload) || '.' ||
    BASE64URL(JWS Signature)

  There is one header segment and one signature segment; the three period-delimited segments admit no second signature and no second header.

- Section 7.1: 'Only one signature/MAC is supported by the JWS Compact Serialization and it provides no syntax to represent a JWS Unprotected Header value.'

Contrast with the JWS JSON Serialization (why the missing syntax matters)

- Section 7.2 defines the JWS JSON Serialization in two forms: the general syntax, which can secure content 'with more than one digital signature and/or MAC operation' via the top-level 'signatures' array, and the flattened syntax for the single signature/MAC case.
- Section 7.2.1 defines the per-signature members 'protected' (BASE64URL(UTF8(JWS Protected Header)), integrity protected) and 'header' (the JWS Unprotected Header as an unencoded JSON object, not integrity protected). The Compact Serialization has no equivalent of the 'header' member and no equivalent of the 'signatures' array.

Practical consequence for implementers

A Compact-serialized JWS is a single-signature/single-MAC, single-header artifact. Any requirement for multiple signatures/MACs (e.g., multi-party signing, algorithm migration with dual signatures, or attaching non-integrity-protected header parameters) cannot be expressed in the Compact Serialization and must use the JWS JSON Serialization (general syntax). A parser for the Compact Serialization should reject input with more than two '.' separators (i.e., anything other than exactly three segments), and must not expect an unprotected header segment.
